text_translated_detailed: From Surat, the 21st February, Anno 1693. — Batavia. To his Excellency the Lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn and the Esteemed Excellencies, the Lords Councillors of Dutch India. Noble and Esteemed, Received on the 30th of the previous month, most manfully, well June 1643 per the ship the steadfastness, namely Gaspersdam, wise, foreseeing, very over Tuticorin and Coromandel. —. Generous Lords, Well Noble, High Commanding Lords. On the day of our departure from Malacca, I have, under the date of 17th January last, most humbly informed your High Excellencies; which letter, and the accompanying box with papers, I trust will have come into your Excellencies' hands; these few lines shall serve only to further inform your High Excellencies that our arrival at the roadstead of Colombo was on the 19th of this month, where we had previously learned that the lord governor of Ceylon had a fleet of eight ships at hand, and from Surat on the 21st February, Anno 1693. — frigates, to which two English ships had also joined themselves, which had been dispatched on the 14th of this month toward Malabar; wherefore, as it has been deemed good by the Ceylonese lord governor and council, your High Excellencies shall come to understand fully from their Excellencies' writing, wherefore I shall conduct myself most humbly in this regard, and shall only mention here that we, in order to advance our voyage and to hasten as much as lies in our power, and likewise in hope of catching up with the fleet at Malabar, today under God's gracious blessing intend to weigh anchor, the lord governor Thomas van Rhee having treated me with all courtesy, for which I am obliged to his Excellency, and I pray God that he may restore his Excellency to his former health, for the greatest service of the Esteemed Company; may that same God grant us a safe and speedy voyage, and preserve us from the haughty

text_translated_detailed: received on the 30th of June 1693 by the Yacht Gaasperdam via Coromandel. From Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693. — Batavia. To His Excellency the Lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Lords, Councilors of the Netherlands India, noble, earnest, highly esteemed, valiant, wise, prudent, most generous Lords. Most Noble, Highly Commanding Lords. On the 21st of February last past, having made ready to continue our journey from the roadstead of Colombo, I humbly reported this to Your Excellency under that date. Contrary winds and currents have delayed our fortunate journey, so that we did not reach Quilon before the 8th of this month after midnight, where we learned from the chief officer Sir Johannes Spilardus that the Lord Commander Isaac van Dielen would betake himself in person to the fleet, in order to observe the Company's interests northward at Wingurla and Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693, in Canara, and to conduct the fleet as far as before Goa, where the four French ships that had been in Surat were staying; and since the chief of Quilon had not yet received any report of the Lord Commander's departure, I deemed it advisable to proceed myself to Cochin by small vessels — thinking whether the Lord Commander might still be there, so that I could meet with His Excellency and deliberate what should be undertaken for the greatest service of the Company; but upon arriving at Cochin I found that the Lord Commander had departed with the fleet on the 8th; concerning His Excellency's intentions, the administrator Vinck could give me no other information than that the Lord Commander had told him orally that he intended to proceed northward with the fleet as far as before Wingurla, and if the French should meet him on the way or before Goa, His Excellency would endeavor to ruin them,

To his Nobility the Mister and Governor-General Willem van Outhoorn, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India. Please, Esteemed, High Respected: the valiant, wise, aforementioned, very generous Gentlemen received in Batavia on the 30th of June by the fluyt Drakenstein over Chormandel: Well Esteemed, High Commanding Gentlemen. On the 23rd of the past month I sent a packet with two original letters dated the 14th and 23rd thereof, signed, together with some enclosures, by the fluyt above Caspel to Tuticorin, consigned to Your High Excellencies; to be further sent from there over Ceylon to Batavia. On the 15th of this month I sent my humble respects with the copies of the aforementioned letters and papers, together with some other enclosures by land to Tuticorin, so that Your High Excellencies, in case the first should be lost, might be served by the second. The present provincial governors have continuously given notice to them through separate letters to Ceylon [Ceijlon], Coromandel [Chormandel], Bengal [Bengalen], Malabar [mallabaer], and Persia. Regarding what invasion the troops of Aurangzeb [orangseel] have committed, they have taken revenge, but through the mediation of this city's governor, everything has been restored to peace, which is to be noted. From Surat on the 28th of May in the year 1693: The Portuguese, in their surrounding lands and villages of Bassein [bassin], have been invaded by the troops of Aurangzeb [orangzeep] under Portuguese lands through Amir Aurangzeb [amarauw mateberchan] in the latter part of the previous year, an invasion which, as it is said, occurred because a certain Mughal or Persian woman, who had become Christian, was hiding under the protection of the Portuguese, and at the request of the aforementioned Amir would not be returned. For revenge of this, the Portuguese arrested all Moorish ships that they could seize, from which, through the intervention of this city's governor Ettematjan [Ettemaatchan], seeing what prejudice His Majesty would suffer here in the tolls, it followed that the aforementioned Portuguese obtained satisfaction and the Moorish ships were also released. Piracy: Two years ago, the following piracy began in earnest in the latter period, from the month of August in the straits of the Red Sea, committed by a European robber, as it is said, against the ships of the wealthy Moorish merchant Molla Abdul Gaffoor [molla abdul gaffoer]. To prevent this and to drive away or destroy the said robber, the governor Ettematjan [Ettemaat Jan] requested a Company's vessel from the governor to prevent such occurrences, as well as from the English and French Company's servants, which was politely declined. And it was respectfully entered in the daily register regarding this matter, which was also refused. There is no suspicion of any ill will from the court regarding our refusal, which we remain obedient to.

text_translated_detailed: Assetchan by order of the Emperor—orangzeep to the duan of this city, dated the 6th of January 1693, in the 36th year of his reign. To the King's duan mierzja mamethalie was delivered, and presented by the chancellor Assetchan by order of the Emperor Orangzeeb, that the governor of Surat, Ettemaatchan, has reported to his Majesty that this year and the previous year the goods of the merchant Abdul Gafoor and several others, together with their ships and all their appurtenances, have been seized and arrested from Surat on the 28th of May in the year 1693, for which reason he found it necessary to summon the heads of the English, French, and Dutch before him, and recommended to them to make a petition to the King to prevent the unknown pirate from his plundering, since the inhabitants were so fearful both for the fleets and otherwise that they dared not continue their trade. However, since this was refused by the aforementioned nations, it will be necessary to forbid them trade entirely, both in Surat as elsewhere, insofar as the King's authority extends. It has been ordered that as long as the aforementioned nations do not suppress the pirate or oppressor, or force him to cease his plundering and do not give him assistance, it has been expressly charged by his Majesty to all the governors as well as the duans of this realm that they shall not be able to grant any license to the aforementioned nations to continue their trade in any way whatsoever. For this reason, Your Excellency is also ordered to take note of this order and to make the King's order felt to those nations insofar as your authority extends. Nothing is expected from the other negligent governors regarding the welfare. He could only catch it because of the prejudice he suffered there, as was first reported after the departure of the ships, it stands to be provided for according to necessity. The aforementioned French vessels, which would have departed on the 21st of April past manned with 800 men from one of France's harbors, had near the Cape of Good Hope captured an English advice cutter called the Samuel destined for Madraspatnam [Madraspatnam: modern equivalent: Madras/Chennai], after great resistance taken, and because of its hopelessness with the crew on board, described by the Captain for 200 pounds sterling under the giving of two officers as common soldiers ransomed. The cited English ship the Elisabeth they captured for the aforementioned enemies 50 miles south of Bombay, and brought here. text_translated_detailed: From Surat on the 20th of May in the year 1693, that I would throw myself into the snares which I so clearly see are laid for me by those who should have patronized me in need and any other contingency, therefore I find myself compelled to make known to Your Excellencies, just as I hereby make known, that I shall be forced to lodge my complaints over Goa and England (although against my will and intention) if Your Excellencies do not be pleased to untie the knot of this hindrance, or if the Honorable gentlemen directors do not be pleased to cut it off, provided that they recognize (as they are expert and experienced merchants) these clear stumbling blocks which they have laid for us in the path of commerce, which their Honors have so kindly paved and opened for us; and since I dare rely infallibly on the virtue of those in whom many make up the body of the most understanding and wisest authorities of the world, as we have experienced in their inscrutable abundant and incomprehensible convenience, wherein they from Surat on the 20th of May in the year 1693 undisputedly may call the cities which they govern the best commerce, having placed the trade in all the accessible world on the footing of a firm stone rock—but as I foresee the cautious judgment and excellent government of Your Excellencies no less than I esteem that same judgment, I deem it unnecessary to expect help from so far away, hoping that Your Excellencies will readily receive in their good favor those who do not make themselves unworthy thereof. (was signed) the same Pedro Pereira. — Batavia To the High Noble Lord Governor-General Willem van Outhoorn and the Noble Lords Council of the Netherlands India. The High Esteemed well-commanding Lords, For the ships the great fishery and Java goes us

text_translated_detailed: From Surat on the 20th of May in the year 1693, undisputedly the cities which they govern may be called the best commerce, having placed the trade in all the accessible world on the footing of a firm stone rock—but as I foresee the cautious judgment and excellent government of Your Excellencies no less than I esteem that same judgment, I deem it unnecessary to expect help from so far away, hoping that Your Excellencies will readily receive in their good favor those who do not make themselves unworthy thereof. (was signed) the same Pedro Pereira. — Batavia To the High Noble Lord Governor-General Willem van Outhoorn and the Noble Lords Council of the Netherlands India. text_translated_detailed: We have now recently received news from the court that His Imperial Majesty, by his own hand, has issued the order to prepare the command letters, so that the general Netherlands Company alone throughout his entire kingdom may exercise their trade everywhere untroubled and at peace, such as Your Esteemed Highness, if it pleases, shall be able to examine in detail. From Surat on the 2nd of October in the year 1693, by means of a translated letter in this regard from the 29th of August, the 14th of the past month, received from the camp at Canauj. According to whose contents we now daily remain awaiting all the mandates to be obtained in copy with great longing, which, once received here, shall be sent with the utmost speed to their respective properly authorized places. The fear raised by us in our aforementioned writing of the last day of July past, by the continuation of further robbery of the Moorish ships of the voyage from here through the Red Sea toward Mocha and such (regarding which that trade has been hindered solely), seems to have largely disappeared, notwithstanding that this year such has again happened to a ship of the merchant Moena Abdul Gaffoor in our aforementioned matter on the return voyage from Jeddah near Bab el-Mandeb, or the Red Sea's strait, by a sea pirate, on account of which the governor, or city magistrate Dittemaetcan, has not brought us any further complaint. From Surat on the 2nd of October in the year 1693, in this regard anew to date. text_translated_detailed: From Japara, First of March 1643. — Bookkeeper Ioannes Ringesaer consigned to the Esteemed Chief Merchant and Head of the General Paymaster's Office Hendrik Dijkman No. 10. A request from the Native Lieutenants Wancobat, Lanang, Jaffar, and Nioman Godek, presented to the Esteemed High Government of India at Japara on the first of March 1693. — Batavia. To the Well Esteemed Sir, Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Well Esteemed, Earnest, Wise, aforementioned. Received on the 23rd of March 1643 by the patchall [a type of vessel]. The Lelij in hand and most generous Gentlemen of the Lieutenants and Engineer Marcus de Baionville, Esteemed High commanding Gentlemen, the Commander Ioan Albert Sloot, is dated the 17th of December last, with the Chialoep [a type of vessel] the Arend over Tagal and Samarang, here arrived well to land, finding the military and further matters still well regulated, inasmuch as the ministers are in a peaceful and good harmony amongst themselves, just as he had left them, whereby we have been brought your Esteemed High respected Letters of the 26th of November before. Since then we have further received your Esteemed High respected Letters of the 24th of December, with the Jagje [a type of vessel] S.r Nicolaes, as well as those of the 15th of January following thereafter, with the Master Carpenter Iurriaen Abrahamsz, over Rimbang, besides all such attachments, Cash, Equipment and other goods, as the received registers and Bills of Lading dictate in that regard: for which and all else, your Esteemed High respected, we humbly thank, the General Office, properly credited has become the aforementioned Chialoep the Arend, we have in accordance with your Esteemed High respected order, dated the 8th of January with a cargo of 88 pieces of house beams and if your Esteemed High would be pleased that we the remaining planks likewise for the Esteemed Company at [uncertain: nenten] or otherwise [uncertain: gem=t] per Asser may allow to stand, First of March 1693.

text_translated_detailed: 35. 10. charged, concerning 2344 pieces of Legger duijgen [wooden staves], dated 13 October 1691, sent from Samarang to Batavia by the fluyt ship Wester Amstel, and which according to the declaration received from the specially commissioned [official] dated 24 December of that same year, were purchased too dearly or were worth no more than one rixdaler [modern equivalent: approximately 2.5 guilders], silver, per piece. — The resident van Wijngaerden writes to us from Rembonq that there, in addition to the round iron already received, there will still be needed about 60 to 70 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 3,600-4,200 kg], a batch of nails, and also 3 pieces of gun carriages with their trunnions, for the newly undertaken work, therefore requesting that Your Excellency's Honors be pleased to have such quantity and type provided at the next opportunity. From Japara—March 1693.—Now as the separate request for rattan mats comes to be indicated herewith, he has also made known to us that a certain small boat anchor, which from the fluyt ship Adrichem in the year past remained lying at that roadstead, after long searching has finally been found again. The interrogatories sent to us dated 26 November last, to be answered at the requisition of Captain Ioan de Moor, we have at once forwarded along with the required order to Surabaya, but since then we have received no writing from there, without doubt because the hard westerly winds do not permit it, their last [letter] to us being from 16 December of the year past, whereby we learn that the masonry work there would be completed within 3 to 4 days, and the fortress thereby so improved that the Mardijker soldiers [modern equivalent: soldiers of mixed descent serving the VOC] were now not considered necessary at all. text_translated_detailed: The Lieutenant Engineer Marcus de Baijonville, having properly inspected the places Japara, Samarang, and Rembang, departs hereby again toward the Coast, in order to bring Your Excellency's Honors the required report concerning their findings, which he would have departed earlier, had not the hard westerly winds and daily tempestuous weather prevented it. It serves meanwhile as honored information to Your Excellency's Honors that we, to satisfy the recently demanded 6 pieces of young strong horses, of 3 to 4 years old, have not yet been able to obtain even one, for those that are somewhat serviceable are seen here now only by chance, and such the Javanese are very reluctant to give up, since the best breed, through much exporting, from Japara, March 1693.—among themselves is scarce, and now much more so than before, it seems, but common stock there is still to be obtained, but we dare not purchase such, as we fear that such would not please Your Excellency's Honors well. Going herewith is a completed account concerning our pay office consigned to the Honored Chief Merchant Hendrik Dijkman, and likewise a request from the Native Lieutenants Wancobat, Lanang, and Godek, to Your Excellency's Honors, with which [document] &. a [uncertain: abbreviation] was signed and was marked: Ioan Albert Sloon, Hendrik Obe, Joann. S Frans, Louis Belleson, M. de Baijonville, Coert Brand, A. I. van der Keurbeek, A. D. Lamsweerde. In the margin stood: Japara, the first of March 1693.—Respectful report to His Excellency, the Honored Lord W. R. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and to Their High Excellency's Honors, the Honored Lords, Counselors of the Netherlands

Also, it is not flanked at all, such that well a thousand men could stand under that mountain without being seen from it, let alone shot at. To this is added that that mountain has no mountain behind it, because it is a ridge of land that extends from within the land to the sea or shore. Although the mountain of the aforementioned ridge of land is separated by a ravine, through which one can pass with ease, and standing on this mountain the buildings themselves fall completely into ruin; indeed, even the walls, so that it appears to be in decay. I believe well that there could be made something good on this mountain, if one were to bring the building materials for it. Mijlen ten anker gekomen digt by de tweede wagt. 7. d. o is bij ons gekomen een kleen prauwtje, verhaelde dan den pangeran matsia Napoera op Latak, ons verwagten soude, en wij op dat seggen geen gelooff wilde slaen hebben wij 'tsamen geresolveert, met die schuijt daerna toe te roeijen, om de regte waerheijt te vernemen gelijk aenstonts met den onderstierman Iom Sluijmer daer na toe stevende, en ontrent 12. uren smiddags daergekomen zijnde, lier Ingabeij Singa lana ons roepen, bij hem gekomen zijnde vonden dallam kotmoeda, zijnde een vande pangeran sijn raads personen, denwelke vriendelijk groete, seggende boven gemelte kotmoeda, dat den pangerom versogt, dat wij daerop tatak soude ten anker komen, alsoo de wegen en revier op Nagabang, toewaren gemaekt, vande Van Japara onder dato P=mo Maart 1693. — tijd
text_translated_detailed: From Japara under date the first of March 1693. — from His Excellency the Governor General and the gentlemen councillors of the Netherlands Indies, which I have been signed by Marcus de Baijonville. Report by the commander of the yacht Cadirij and Sergeant Valentijn Pieter Hagenberg, concerning their meeting at Balemboong on the 27th of September 1692. After receiving orders from Captain Joan Bervelt, we departed with six soldiers to the yacht Cadirij, sent to bring the Balemboong ambassadors to their lord and master, and by the help of God, we set sail in the afternoon and arrived toward evening on the 28th of the same month near Passourouan, on the 29th at the mouth, on the 30th before Cape Sandana, on the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of December. We continued as above with tacking. From Japara under date — the first of March 1693. On the 4th we advanced a little, on the 5th to about 4 miles from Latak, on the 6th with favorable current, passing Tatak about 4 miles we came to anchor near the second watch. On the 7th a small prau came to us, reporting that the Pangeran Matsia Napoera at Latak would be expecting us, and we did not want to believe this report, so we resolved together to row there in that boat to learn the true facts, just as immediately with the under-steersman Iom Sluijmer heading there, and arriving there around 12 o'clock in the afternoon, Ingabeij Singa lana called us over, and when we came to him we found Dallam Kotmoeda, being one of the Pangeran's council members, who greeted us in a friendly manner, saying that the aforementioned Kotmoeda reported that the Pangeran requested that we anchor at Tatak, since the roads and river at Nagabang had been made passable. From Japara under date the first of March 1693. —

We took our leave from Ingabeij Singalana and other envoys, and they complained to us of their distress, that the Pangeram had caused their krises and spears to be taken away in the first instance, wishing thereby to demonstrate that he was presently lord and master, and that it stood in his will to allow their status to be—maintained, but after our departure, they would have to surrender the same, and recover their weapons again, saying that Singalana would send envoys to Batavia again in a month or four weeks. From Japara under date [of] March 1693, [on the] 9th, 10th, and 11th of December: we were not lacking water and firewood. Around midday Souroan called us to come to him at dallam pitsiarakan, which we immediately went ashore to do. Upon coming to him, he gave us the letter from the Pangeran, as well as the account to be made to their Excellency and the gentlemen councillors of India, and wished us good fortune and safe passage. Thanking him, we took our leave and proceeded to the ship. On the 12th, in the morning of the day, with the help of God and a favorable wind and current, under the firing of three cannon shots we set sail, and that same evening came past Cape Pandana. On the 13th, past Pamimaroekan. On the 14th, past the mouth. On the 15th, between Quanjer and Passouroan. On the 16th, here at this place, proceeding further to land; to make report to Your Excellency of our experiences, as we hereby fulfill through this writing. Was undersigned, Valentijn Pieter Hagenberg, in Marginestont, in the Yacht Cadiij, 16th and December 1683.

text_translated_detailed: First of March 1693.—From Japara under date. Translation of a Javanese Letter, by the Balemboangan Pangeran, Matsia Napoera, to their Esteemed Excellency at Batavia, sent from there originally via Surabaya and Japara, received here on the 23rd of March 1693. This letter comes from me, Pangeran Adipattij of Balemboangan, to make known that the pangawas [officers] of the Pangeran Adipattij of Balemboangan, who are named Angabeij Singalana, Angabeij Ebira Diaga, Angabeij Joerengmanoen, and Loera Singabaija, have here arrived safely with the gifts they brought with them, for which I am grateful to the Company. The goods sent over have been received by me: a gilded snaphaun [flintlock musket], a pair of pistols, a gilded hewing tool, three Chinese cloths, two fine Moorish scarlets, red phelp [uncertain: original term], and half a case of rose water. And after having thanked the Company once more, I shall say that if one wishes to engage in commerce, buying and selling, that I am inclined to do so from Japara under date—First of March 1693. This letter is sent by the Pangeran Adipattij of Balemboangan. Register of the papers which on this day per the Yacht the St. Nicolaes are being sent to Batavia, consigned to the well-esteemed Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. text_translated_detailed: shows, but around Semarang [Samarang] it had rained quite heavily until the 22nd of March, making it difficult to begin the rice harvest, especially since no barrel staves [wooden barrel components] had arrived up to that point, as is confirmed by the writing of the resident Abraham Smesser, a copy of which is also attached here. The ship De Grijpvogel [The Goshawk], destined for Ternate, arrived at the roadstead here on the 9th of last month to obtain a new rudder, since his had broken after departing from Batavia. We provided him with one as soon as possible, but due to the strong currents that prevail in this bay at that time of year, it took a good three or four days before he could receive it on board and be ready with it. Moreover, it was a narrow escape from shipwreck, for they had already lost three anchors before Japara on the 17th of April 1693, and had come so close to the rocky shore as was ever dangerous. However, when the weather improved, on the 13th following they managed to get under sail again, leaving one anchor behind, which they were forced to cut loose. We have since made several fruitless attempts to fish for it, and with the arrival of favorable weather, further attempts are planned. A certain Castilian captain named Manuel Gallan, with his prau [a type of sailing vessel] from Manila, wanting to go to Banjarmasin, found upon his arrival there three Portuguese ships at war with the local inhabitants, and was therefore forced to leave the harbor. From there he came here with the intention of having his prau caulked somewhat, or if possible, to have a rudder made in the European manner in place of the native one. As far as we have been able to ascertain, their capital consists partly of Manila tobacco and 40,000 Mexican reales [Mexican silver coins].

The bookkeeper Barent Mulder, who arrived here in December last by way of Sirebon [Cirebon] in a native vessel, has since his arrival shown that he is not only a great drunkard and an impertinent, troublesome person, but also that he sometimes, with the new or full moon, when he is sober, suffers such dangerous and irrational intervals that we have had to store various sharp objects from the assistants' room (where he lodged along with the other officers) elsewhere at night. Besides many other whims that he sometimes directs toward the local inhabitants, which are entirely inappropriate, so that we deemed it necessary to have him depart from here again to Batavia, which is hereby done, in hope and trust that Your Honored Excellency will be pleased to regard this as well done. Likewise, the ensign Jan Eduard van der Schuer, on account of his capricious and irritable nature, sent from Japara on the 17th of April 1643 [likely 1693] to Surabaya, now also departs with the aforementioned vessel.

For since he has not only at Surabaya, but over several years at Tagal, Semarang, here and elsewhere, shown his impertinence in abundance, we regard him as entirely unsuitable here for cultivating the common peace. And likewise departs the young surgeon Anthony Paulus, in order to be examined there according to Your Honored Excellency's esteemed command, as well as the corporal Jeppe Jellis, who has for a long time earnestly requested to go to Batavia in order to receive the holy baptism there, which we could not refuse him, although the garrison has in the meantime become quite weakened through the successive deaths of the post holders. The assistants Albert Proper, who has now for a full year managed the equipment books and the shop, as well as the transfer of the business books, and Johannes Ringesaer, who has managed the soldiers' pay books here at the office, both request Your Honored Excellency, by their petitions enclosed herewith, to obtain a favorable improvement in rank and salary. And since both of them are officers of good competence and suitable deportment, we cannot refrain from likewise humbly requesting that they may be granted a favorable endorsement by Your Honored Excellency's great goodness.

text_translated_detailed: The Malay Captain named Intje Poetij has presented to us the complaints which he and his people have lodged regarding the unbearable harassment that they claim has been inflicted upon them by the present Captain Bagus Salim, and has submitted this to Your Esteemed Honour. Upon this matter, a thorough investigation has been conducted here by expressly appointed commissioners, namely Lieutenant Jan van der Keurbeek, Ensign Anthonij de Lamsweerde, and first Sergeant Rutger Valentijn, but up to now it has not been found that anyone among that nation has any knowledge whatsoever of the matters which the aforementioned Radin Oijoe puts forward in the aforementioned petition, as Your Esteemed Honour will be pleased to see from the written report of the cited commissioners attached herewith, regarding what they have been able to ascertain in this matter, and to which we have conducted ourselves with deference in this regard on account of brevity. From Japara on the 20th of May 1693. We add here only that which concerns the aforementioned Orijoe, regarding the arrest of one of their Nachodas [ship captains], who had already received a sealed pass to Batavia from the Commander, comes to be retrieved, and also this matter is not as they represent it there, but it has always been a custom here that the passes for all Malays and Macassarese were issued by their Captains or their people, in order to keep the daily traffic of all manner of foreign people out of the Company's lodge or fortification. Against this, a certain Intje Batoea, a subordinate of the aforementioned Radin Oijoe, has on diverse occasions taken it upon himself, contrary to custom, to issue passes for others of his nation, as if he had been authorized to do so, on account of which the present Captain Lutchie Salim finally addressed him once and brought him before the Commander to ascertain by whose order he did this, which the Captain had expressly ordered him always to attend to when the Commander, as mentioned, also said the aforementioned Lutchie Batoea, from Japara

text_translated_detailed: Since the aforementioned small vessel was found to be in such poor condition from below that no effort or expense of repair could help it, we have deemed it most advantageous for the Company's benefit to have the empty hull left there in such a manner, fully submerged in water, to be sold to the highest bidding Chinese (who might have the speculation to burn out the ironwork and sell it, which we have for that purpose had the inhabitants of Samarang and hereabouts notified by proclamation that this shall take place on the first Monday in July coming here, which we hope and trust will not displease Your Honour, in view of the fact that with longer delay one would not only be compelled to keep watch there against the brackish water, against all robbers or other willful persons, but one would also have to fear that the same, with the passage of time from Japara on the 29th of June 1693, by some northerly winds through the Sea, might come to be entirely destroyed. The ship's equipment, goods both good and bad as they are, we have for the most part had unloaded from the wreck and secured here, but since the small ship lies completely on its side and full of water, the seafaring men see no chance of getting the large and foresail mast out whole, although the aforementioned mast is only of Jati wood and nothing particularly special; nevertheless we shall have everything done in that regard that is possible, and the entire fleet, since we have no suitable place here to store it, at the first opportunity of ship's space, to send to Your Honour, whereupon then also, for further verification, the required information regarding the circumstances concerning the stranding and loss of the aforementioned small vessel shall come, in total the free merchant Johannes Moors has, during his presence here, paid into the Company's Cash the sum of 1000.

text_translated_detailed: letter from the Resident Smetser we received, whereby the same made known that at that place, under the authority of the former Batavian Lieutenant named Quepaukwa, the day before yesterday near the dwelling of the fellow Chinese Toomko, a group of that nation had gathered together and caused great fear among the people from Japara on the 30th of June 1693, having taken the road to Cirebon or elsewhere, and also that they had violently dragged away some women and children, and had killed a man in passing, just as all of this is to be seen in detail from the said Resident's copy of his writing herewith attached; without one having been able to learn to this point, in truth, what exactly the intention of the said conspirators may be, or who their further adherents are, yet it is clear enough that here on the coast everywhere, a great number of ruffians and all manner of scum of the Chinese, as well as other nations, are present, who are not much to be trusted, and it is possible that the said gathered ruffians, so hastily without first attempting anything, chose the hateful path, because they, as the principal ones of more unknown dependents, discovering themselves from some earlier suspicion regarding one or another treacherous design, did not dare to await the appointed time of execution, but what the true truth of it is shall time need to reveal further: Meanwhile we have strengthened the Samarang Office with another 12 soldiers, 6 sailors, some gunpowder and hand grenades &c., just as we also shortly sent a letter to the Sousouh, from Japara on the 30th of June 1693, with the request that he be pleased to issue orders to pursue the said fugitives and to bring them into our hands if it be possible, how he shall now conduct himself in this regard, we shall endeavor to learn in due time.

Another private letter by way of Quehuijqua, a Chinese in Samarang, from Nuepanko and Quetoanko, leaders of a group of rebellious Chinese, have sent a Quetienco to other surrounding places in order to gather elsewhere some ill-willed and disobedient mutineers, in order to undertake with them a desperate assault on the Chinese living here and on the Company's lodge. This was planned and was to be carried out in such a manner that on the 25th day of this 5th month, around midday, 30 accomplices among themselves would begin a violent fight, at which time the aggrieved parties would run to the Company's lodge in order to complain to the governor about the violence and suffered damage, and to seek justice. These complainants would then be attacked and killed by the Hollanders. Another forty persons of this cursed conspiracy would meanwhile set the village on fire on all sides; the opponents, who would have promised them this, would kill and further enrich themselves from the plunder of these houses. But God willed that on that day this accursed work would be blessed, for around midday there fell a heavy downpour of rain that dampened everything, so that they could not carry out their plan at that appointed time. However, toward evening they departed to the house of the Chinese Cotianko. He had been asked to make flags for them, and when he refused, they beheaded him in his house and killed him. And this unholy deed having been completed, they departed together, approximately 100 armed Chinese, followed by women and children, toward Mataram. What evil may yet come to us from there, we do not know. We are sending to Kiauko in order to make this deed quickly known to the High government in Batavia, so that timely redress might be made and carried out. text_translated_detailed: Dated 12 July 1693. Since I could not help my child, I would be ashamed if I heard of other Kings' children, therefore I request that this Nakhoda panda, my child, may follow, since he is also of the people, of Captain Malaijo, whom one can also believe on my behalf, for through this, if any deficiency or difficulty should arise, we can also request our masters for help. text_translated_detailed: From Japara the 1st of August 1693. Batavia. To the well-honored Lord Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the honored Lords Council of the Dutch Indies. Per the jacht the Gideon received on the 6th of August 1693 — Most esteemed, honored, and valiant Lords. Just as we informed Your Lordships' high honor on the 23rd of the recently passed month with the Chaloupe the Eagle, among other things, that the Tommogon Tsiakra Nagara, after sending some more imprisoned Chinese, would soon follow: so he also came that same day, together with a party of mantris and other retinue from Semarang, to land here, and the next day appeared in the Company's Lodge, also bringing a Javanese missive from the Pangeran Depati Anom to Commander Sloot, wherein the same relates to the Principal how he had determined that, if the scattered Chinese came to reach the east, they would certainly have fled to Surapati, for which reason he had gone out in person against them and captured them by the Solo River, but he had not wished to kill them in consideration of the overseas peoples who, here on Java according to Contract, stood under the Jurisdiction of the Company. [modern equivalent: 519 guilders, 6 stuivers, 4 penningen], as well as a parcel of small round timber, pampens and barrel work, from the standing jacht [small ship] the Craanvogel, just as the bill of lading and invoice herewith will show. And so also now travel over the remaining ship's personnel of the aforementioned small vessel, whose account also goes beside here, along with a separate name roll with indication of how and where all the same departed or remained, besides that there also travels a certain soldier Anthony Clarisse, who from the sloop the Eagle remained here standing, and gave himself up the next day after departure, with the notification that he through a certain assault (by which he was also affected) against somewhere fell asleep and thereby to his sorrow sailed out behind. Likewise have we, since the occasion presents itself for this, besides for the aforementioned timber works in the incoming vessel, also shipped off a quantity of 4900 pounds of spoiled gunpowder, consisting of 49 small barrels. Writing thus far, the ship Coeverden appears here with Your Honored Excellency's esteemed letters of the 17th of the month just past, upon which the required response per return next opportunity is to follow. With which &c. undersigned and was signed I:

text_translated_detailed: From Japara under date 1st August 1642. — Extract day register kept at the head office Japara under date 24th and 25th July 1693. This forenoon the Tommogon and afgfam [uncertain: possibly a title or name] of the Susuhunan Tsiaca Nagara, with his fellow called Poespanagara, Demang Malang, Natta Juda, and Tsitra Juda, by order of the Honored Mister Commander Ioan Albert Sloot, through the first clerk Rutgert Voelentijn, and the Captain of the free Malays, from the forecourt of the governor of this place Inwaraga, fetched, and brought within the company's lodge to audience with his Excellency in the upper hall, and received with proper respect by his Excellency, the Honored Captain Ram and Merchant Hendrick Obe, as when the aforementioned Tommogon Tsiaca Nagara, after the aforementioned Honored ones and his people were seated in order, under the firing of 13 cannon shots, delivered a Javanese missive, by the Pangeran Adij Pattij, in the name of his father the Susuhunan, to the aforementioned his Excellency, which being received with courtesy, was immediately translated, and they found it to read as follows: Translation of Malay missive by the Pangeran Adij Pattij Anum, son of the Susuhunan, in Javanese to the Honored Mister Commander Ioan Albert Sloot at Japara, dated August 1st, 1693, and on the 24th July 1643, brought by the Tommogon Tsiaca Nagara and some other courtiers and delivered there. text_translated_detailed: Councillors of the Netherlands India Most Esteemed, Honored, Venerable, Mighty, Wise, Foresighted, Most Generous Gentlemen Most Esteemed Honored Commanding Gentlemen In our most recent humble [communication] of the previous month of August we informed Your Excellency's Highness with the fluyt ship the Gidion of the arrival of the ship Coeverden, as was our duty. text_translated_detailed: From Japara on the 4th of October 1693. Even with cannon, no damage could be inflicted, being along the beach in this bay of Torboija to the east, and Carninganijer, to the west of the river of Samarang, so soft and muddy that the ships, if necessary, could run against the shore without any difficulty, and could protect themselves without anchors or ropes. If it pleases Your Excellency to find it good to send here a gang along with a party of carpenters, masons, five or six sawyers, shovels and spades, etc., then all the woodwork for the dwelling and warehouses, under covered sheds, could be conveniently completed during this coming rainy monsoon, and meanwhile the rivers could be diverted or dug out, the ground raised, and everything prepared so that the work could be brought into a state of use at the beginning of the coming east monsoon season. For which reason we await Your Excellency's esteemed sentiment. Furthermore, uncle, you have requested the release of the imprisoned Chinese, their wives and children, or those from Pauqua. I am pleased that you have demanded this of me, and I am also inclined to follow uncle's desire, but I request your help and power regarding those two children, whom I have taken as my own. The ones whom I have now dismissed from the Company's service are the oerod Jalangs, with the Loera gandek, and likewise also poesparaga, whom I have entrusted. Regarding the fifty armed Chinese, the hoes and guns which you sent us with the aforementioned Poesparaga, they are well placed, and I have delivered them to the Susuhunan, who has received them with great difficulty and gratitude from Japara under date 4th of October 1693, as he places much trust in you. And since you, uncle, have requested of us that we interrogate the woman khinitie, we would have been inclined to do so, but now that all the Chinese have come bound, we can learn from them who called upon them, whether I or the Susuhunan, according to Rangas's account. text_translated_detailed: All the Chinese have come bound, so we can learn from them who called upon them, whether I or the Susuhunan, according to Rangas's account. I deliver to you your Toamko, whom you can interrogate; and if there is any sign that I or the Padoeka Susuhunan called upon her, then learn that thoroughly, for I know nothing of it, nor have I heard anything, but I have understood from the Company that they were at Angaroncg, and also from your letter, when this became entirely clear at Cartazoura, and then Hoamko had already been at Carta Zoura. I have told Toomko at Coirta Soura that he came here with the foreknowledge of the Esteemed Company to pay the tax of Caring Hanjer, which he did. After which he appeared before the Padoeka Susuhunan, and having spoken with him, he went back to Caring Hanjer. Meanwhile, news came that the Chinese Toankos had also taken his people, wanting to kill them, and that Toanko, traveling back, had cried out. From Japara under date 4th of October 1693. And uncle, why would I have let Toomko go away if it were my fault? And why would I then send you those Chinese alive? And I assure you, if it had been my doing, I would not have sent them all, for then the words would not mean much. text_translated_detailed: I request you that you interrogate Toanko thoroughly on the Company's behalf, for he is an old servant of the Susuhunan and of you, yes, even when the Susuhunan was still the Pattij, and Toanko is his wealth and his body also belongs to the Susuhunan. Toonko went to Cartasoera for profit, but Ronga Samarang has given him a bad name. Therefore, uncle, it is the Susuhunan's desire that Ranga Samarang be relieved of his office, which the Susuhunan trusts that you will cause to happen, and when the Commander has done this, then he can, if it pleases him, place someone else in his place, or choose someone here at Cartasoura or at Samarang for it, which would be agreeable to him; for he leaves this to you, and if Kiauko no longer comes to pay as he has still done yearly, then we will also let him lose his position, for his three years have now already passed. Previously I requested that the Sumanappers could also march up to defend Souropattij on those From Japara under date 4th of October 1693. — without giving weapons to Souropattij, and that the Sampanders who do not want to fight find no refuge at that place, for the passive or coastal peoples would become angry about it. Therefore I still await your trust regarding this; and if the works of Samarang and Sumanap are not completed, then the Susuhunan will be ashamed, and then more evil will happen. And since Catip Calij is dead, and he had a thousand men, from whom the Esteemed Company took over the woodworks (according to their value), I hope that nevertheless, as before, his progress will continue. Jalants vaert. ontfangen Ed:, Erntfste, Ho: agtb:, manhafte, den 16. 9ber 1693. — wijse, voorsz:, genereuse Heren wel Ed: Ho: gebiedende Heren Met de schepen hendrik Maurits en Coeverden zijn uEd: Ho: agtb: g'eerde letteren, vanden 15. en 8. n october, den 19. daeraen volgende, alhier wel aengebragt, en daer besijden ook zoodanig Contanten en goederen, als de mede gekomene facturas, dierwegen ten bedrage van ƒ78475. 8. —. dicteren; voor welk bedraegen het generael, behoorlijk gecrediteert staet te werden. de schepen voornoemt leggen thans om hunne ladinge tot Samarang, en de qualle damak, in te nemen, alwaer wij meijnen, alhoewel dit kloeke bodems zijn, dat wel zoo veel houtwerken resteren sullen, om boven dien, nog een gemeen bodem vol te konnen steken, maer het is te dugten, na het zig aen laet zien, off de weste moessen ons niet te vroeg belopen zal, om hetselve nog te konnen doen afhalen, ten aensien men alhier bij menschen geheugen in't oosterzaijsoen, noijt Van Japara den 5:en November 1693 zoo veel regen, en onstuijnicg weer, als dit Iaer vernomen heeft, om welke redenen wel ten principalen, wij ons Iegenwoordig ook buijten staet bevinden om uEd: agtb: het gevorderde zour van rimbang, off elders toeschicken; wan de overvloedige regen, die hier doorgaens gevallen is, heeft het zoutmaken zodanig verhindert, datter thans nauwlijx een Coijang van 'tselve voor geld te bekomen zij, zulx dat de prijs van 't gene men over een Iaer off 2. voor 1½ off 2. rd. s pleeg te kopen, nu alboven de 12. rijxd. s steijgt En dewijle het schip Coeverden, van bovenen ondigt geoordelt werd, om in dees tijd, die smeltende ziltigh.
text_translated_detailed: From Japara, the 5th of November 1693. Batavia. To the well-esteemed Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India. Prince Jalants voyage. Received, esteemed, earnest, high-honored, valiant, on the 16th of September 1693 — wise, aforementioned, generous Gentlemen, well-esteemed, high-honored, commanding Gentlemen. With the ships Hendrik Maurits and Coeverden, your esteemed high-honored letters, dated the 15th and 8th of October, have been brought here well on the 19th following, and besides that also such cash and goods, as the accompanying invoices dictate, to the amount of ƒ78,475.8.—. For which amount the general account is to be properly credited. The aforementioned ships now lie at Samarang to take on their cargo and the quality damask, where we believe, although these are sturdy vessels, that there will indeed be so much timber remaining that we could still load one more common vessel on top of it, but it is to be feared, as it appears, whether the western winds will not come upon us too early to be able to still have it hauled away, considering that here in the memory of men in the eastern season, never from Japara on the 5th of November 1693 has so much rain and stormy weather been experienced as this year, for which reasons principally we find ourselves presently unable to send your esteemed high-honored the demanded salt from Rimbang or elsewhere; for the excessive rain that has fallen here continuously has so hindered salt-making that now scarcely a coyang [a measure of salt] of the same can be obtained for money, such that the price of what one used to buy a year or two ago for 1½ or 2 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch silver coins] now rises above 12 rixdollars. And since the ship Coeverden is judged from above to be unsuitable to carry in this time the melting salty—

text_translated_detailed: Received from Sumapap on 19 November 1693 — to His Excellency the Honorable Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Lords Councillors of India at Batavia, and so forth, which served as an escort for this letter from the angabeij [local chief] bradja pattij, who was sent by me to appear before Your Excellency's Honors with some fruits from the lands of Sumapap and Pamankassam. These consist of the following gift, namely: 10 picols [modern equivalent: approximately 600 kg] of cotton, being in each picol 1000 bundles; 5 loads of green cadjonrg [uncertain: type of textile or material]; 50 pots filled with clappus oil; 3000 pieces of stone bream fish; 30 pots with bladjang [uncertain: type of spice or condiment]; 15 of the same with eel; and 100 pieces of loaded snaphanen [uncertain: type of wood or material] of angasamen wood. With the request that this small amount may be accepted, furthermore requesting that the Radeen Aria Poelandjeuwa, that Your Excellency's Honors be pleased to favor him with a diamond ring, Bengali spectacles, sadour oil, tin, and lead, nutmeg and rose water. Everything that Radeen Aria Poelandjeuwa has to say is known to father bradja pattij. Ending: — Register of the papers which on this day per the ship Coeverden [ship name] are being sent to Batavia, consigned to the Honorable Lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Lords Councillors of India. A name list of some women, children, slave women and pledges of the executed Chinese, of which some have now been transferred and per the next more are to follow. 4. Two cases with closed business and folded account books, according to their separate registers contained therein marked &=&. 5. An open letter

text_translated_detailed: From Japara, 13 November 1693. Batavia. To the Honorable Lord M. W. van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Lords Councillors of India per the ship Coeverden. Honorable, Esteemed, Honored, Valiant, Received 25 September 1693. Wise, aforementioned, and generous Lords, Your Honors commanding. On the 5th of this month, on our behalf, such reports have been sent to Your Honors per domestic voyage as is respectfully evidenced by the copy herewith, since then the Commander Sloot with the ship Coeverden from Samarang has appeared here again, just as the Chialoep the Arend [ship name] with Your Honors' esteemed letters of the 28th of the previous month has arrived, besides two house carpenters and 5 pieces of Pienang wood oar shafts, but the metal block that should have been there, says the helmsman of the aforementioned Chialoep, he did not receive there, which now also will not need to be sent after, since here at Japara a suitable block has already been made, and more of the like can be made, if the same should come to be lacking. And since from the aforementioned Your Honors' letters it appears how Almighty God has been pleased to bless the Company's weapons against our enemies in the capturing of the fortress, we shall cause the due thanksgiving to be made to the Heavenly Father regarding the same, and likewise with joy shall make it known among the natives everywhere. The aforementioned Chialoep the Arend we shall send first to Rembang in order to obtain its cargo there, since there are now no planks in stock here, in accordance with Your Honors' command, and then subsequently proceed to Makassar. Just as the ship Coeverden now comes to Your Honors with the following cargo, namely 222 pieces of beams in sort; 6350 — legger

'n November 1693. appostil, mag komen te erlangen den Cap.:n der Chinesen oijpinko alhier, heeft ons versogt, om op de bekomen Licentie van VHoEd agtb: als nu voor een springtogje na batavia te mogen gaen; maer alsoo wij zijn persoon, bij dese Conjecture, hier als nog nodig agten, zoo hs hem sulx in't welnemen van VEd agtb: voor ditmael afgeslagen, onder toesegginge wanneer de samarangsen Sabandaer kiauko van Costij gereverteert sal wesen, dan hij als dan sal mogen vertrecken . den baes Timmerman Iurriaen abrahams, versoekt dat de roer haep, en vingerlingen voor de I. o aenbevolene Chialoepen, van 55. â 56. voeten, Conform de rotting niatjes hiernevens gaende gemaekt en hem toegsonden mogen worden, gelijk hij ook wel wenschte, dat vEd agtb: hem soo spoedig als doenlijk zij, zodanige spijkers en andere benodigtheden, beliefde te laten toekomen, als de apparte notitie dierwegens hier besijden, komt aente wijsen . waer mede ko onderstont en was getekent. Ioan albert sloot, Hendrik obe, Marcus de baijonville Lourens Timmerling, en anth: de Lamsweerde, ter zijdeston Japara den 13. en November 1693. Eerbiedig rapport aenden wel Ed: Heer M=r Willem van Outhoorn gouverneur generael en de Ed: heren raden van India, wegens Van Samarang den 7. November 1893. het verkiesen en afsteken van een plaets tot een beknopte vastigheijt of fortificatie op de revier van Samarang, door den Luijtenant en Ingenieur, Marcus de Baijawille, van haer HoEd: met een schriftel: Commissie daer toe gecommitteer wel Ed: Ho: gebiedende Heren den 2:en september Laestleden met de Chialoep padang van Jappara Batavia na bartavia gevaren, zijn wij den 20. d. o daer gearriveert, en met dE Heer Command. r Ioan albert sloor, van VEd: Ho: agtb: g'eerde Commissie gesprooken hebbende, ben ik door zijn Ed: ordre den 23. d. o met deselvige
text_translated_detailed: From Japara on the 13th of November 1693. A postscript: the Captain of the Chinese, Oijpinko, here present, has requested us, in order to obtain the license received from Your Honored Excellency, to be permitted to make a short journey to Batavia; but since we consider his person, by this conjecture, still necessary here, we have for this time refused him such permission, with the assurance that when the Samarang Sabandaer Kiauko from Costij shall have returned, he may then depart. The master carpenter Iurriaen Abrahams requests that the rudder hoop and finger-timbers for the aforementioned Chialoeps [small vessels] of 55 to 56 feet, made conforming to the timber patterns sent herewith, may be made and sent to him, just as he also wished that Your Honored Excellency would be pleased to send him, as soon as possible, such nails and other necessities as the separate note concerning this matter, attached hereto, comes to indicate. Wherewith it was understood and signed. Ioan Albert Sloot, Hendrik Obe, Marcus de Baijawille, Lourens Timmerling, and Anth: de Lamsweerde, at the side of Japara on the 13th of November 1693. Respectful report to the Well-Honored Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Honored gentlemen counselors of India, concerning the selection and marking out of a place for a small fortification on the river of Samarang, by the Lieutenant and Engineer Marcus de Baijawille, commissioned thereto by Your Honored Excellency with a written commission, Well-Honored commanding gentlemen, on the 2nd of September last, with the Chialoep Padang from Japara to Batavia we traveled to Batavia, and on the 20th of this month we arrived there, and having spoken with the Mister Commander Ioan Albert Sloot, of Your Honored Excellency's esteemed commission, I was by his order on the 23rd of this month

Thus the good opinion which I had gained of that ground through boring was taken from me again by the driving, and since the ground is soft clay, it has been ordered that good sufficient planks, 4½ to 5 inches thick and 8 to 9 broad, be laid in the ground, 3½ feet deep, with respect to the berm, and 4 feet with respect to the inner ground, in order to set palisades upon them, whereby they will then, in my judgment, not be able to sink. Also, the ground within the fortification will be 1½ feet higher than that of the berm, whereby the water can run off and drain so much the better. The batteries for the cannon come in the bastions or points, which must be 15 to 16 feet broad, so that the cannon can be drawn out from there, and one can load it from within. I had ordered palisades to be cut long 17 feet and thick 6 inches square; but before my arrival, already being entrusted to the natives, they were to deliver them 16 feet long and 7 to 8 thick, and because those that lie cut here all together are quite fully 16 feet, and that they nevertheless come to cost, with respect to their thickness, according to the saying of the resident Mister Smetser, so one lets them continue as they are, saving that I have done the above under Your Honored Excellency's wiser judgment and "bien benne poligone" (being finished) 12 1/8 rods long, has been drawn and measured, so that one may thereafter or in time according to Your Well-Honored Excellency's pleasure build another five-cornered fort. From Samarang on the 7th of November 1693.

text_translated_detailed: Received on 7 March 1695 by native vessel from Bantam on 5 March 1693 Batavia. To the Most Esteemed and Honored Sir Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen of the Council of the Netherlands Indies, Esteemed and Most Earnest, Most Honorable, Valiant, Wise, Aforementioned, and Most Generous Gentlemen, Most Esteemed and Most Commanding Gentlemen. In accordance with Your Esteemed Orders, I have conferred with the realm administrator concerning the matter of pepper, and deliberated with the others in what manner it would be possible to increase the supply. The realm administrator was at first reluctant to have those from Lampung present on this subject, of whom only two chiefs from Lampung were present in the place, so as not to incur the King's displeasure, of which he made known that the reasons were sufficiently understandable and could not be unknown to me, as I had met with His Excellency several times, in that His Excellency the Sultan on the Sunda Strait was pleased to see, and the matter let slip, with respect to the arrived Lampungers from Bantam on 5 March 1693—their pepper having been unloaded, under the guise of the Company's service they were detained and received no payment; if they could make two voyages home, this would deter such people and it would be more profitable, also for the enlargement of the Sultan's domains, if those people were not detained, but after the pepper vessels were unloaded, the Sultan paid the pepper merchants regularly and without delay, they were sent back again. His Excellency's opinion being apprehended by me, he made known that he saw no chance this year to be able to deliver as much pepper as in the past year, but that according to his estimate for this year, that would amount to 5,000 bahars [modern equivalent: approximately 300,000 kg], unless the supply of pepper from previous years and that which by the drought of the upland streams and canals, as well as high water falls, on the occasion of their swelling, was carried away extraordinarily, assuring that there still remained over 2, 3, or 4 years, great quantities through the inability of the cultivators and pepper planters, and on occasion it was asked to have those carried away, and from Bantam on 5 November 1643, that by the frequent swelling of the rivers, His Excellency let it be understood that the delivery could be estimated at 7,000 bahars, but as that depended on the falling of water from the sky, he could say nothing further than to leave such to time. His Excellency was surprised that with the King he was strongly urged to excuse the pepper merchants from court service and to encourage those people more and more to grant some increase, even if it were ¼ Spanish real [modern equivalent: a quarter of a Spanish silver coin] per bahar more, promising that he would second it with the King and advise His Majesty thereto, as understanding that the King's domains would find that profitable, declaring further that when the Spanish money from Batavia had come, with great difficulty the King had to be disposed to make some payment, and that His Excellency on behalf of the Sultan was left with just enough in hand to be able to pay for ten bahars

text_translated_detailed: From Bantam on the 6th of March 1643. Batavia. To the Well Honored Sir Joan van Hoorn, first Councilor and Director General of the Netherlands Indies. Honored, greatly esteemed, aforementioned, most generous Gentlemen. Honored and strict Sir. Today the King requested 200 pounds of various types of small nails, namely 6 pound, 4 pound, 3 pound, and 2 pound varieties, as well as tinned nails and greyish nails in assorted types. These cannot be found here, nor have they arrived with the last request, by which means this will serve no other purpose than to request of Your Honored Excellence, in the name and on behalf of the Sultan, that by the first opportunity they may be sent hither. For the first 200 pounds of the aforementioned type of small nails, and to Your Honored Excellence it is not from Bantam on the 6th of March 1693 a daily burden to have to trouble you, my humble request is that Your Excellency be pleased to order that in total 400 pounds may come to us, so that we may be provided with something of it for a while. Today, besides the pepper mentioned in my writing of yesterday to the Honored Excellency, the general and Honored Council of India, another 80 bales of pepper have been brought, so that I trust for the arrival of the vessel, which we expect to meet around the 12th of this month, we shall again have a good cargo in reserve. With which, etc. Signed and was signed Edmond van Sterrevelt, on behalf of Bantam, 6th March 1693. Batavia to the Well Honored Sir M. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honored Council of the Netherlands Indies.

text_translated_detailed: From Bantam on the 21st of March 1693 to Batavia. To His Excellency the Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Most Esteemed, Mighty, Wise, Aforementioned, and Most Generous Lords, Your Highness and Excellency. Strict Steven (not to detain you long herewith, we therefore refer ourselves to the enclosed letter herein, which was brought here shortly from the ship Thuijs te Loo, and sent hither by Commander P. Huntum, subscribed to Your Highness and Excellency, which in accordance with the previous Orders, has been opened and read, by express courier, for Your Excellency's Highness and Excellency's further proceedings). The E. Chief arrived here only the day before yesterday, and the yacht Andromeda, which has been unloaded of the effects he brought, shall without delay be fully laden with the Camhout [teak wood], pure rope, from Bantam on the 21st of March 1693, and lampongs pepper, in order to turn the bow toward Batavia at the earliest opportunity. And since tomorrow one of His Majesty's vessels is to navigate from here to fetch coastal cloths from there, under the supervision of Kiaij Aria Raja Segdana, with our letter likewise to proceed therewith, we conclude this matter. It was signed Admunt van Sterrevelt, beside which stood Bantam on the 21st of March 1691. And the postscript stood: P.S. Upon the closing of this letter, the ship has advanced above the Island Panjang, whither to send refreshments, with the recommendation that they perform their duties to the perfecting of the voyage to Batavia to the Highness and Excellency the Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Most Esteemed, Mighty, Wise, Aforementioned, Most Generous Lords.

Courant soo verschijnt hiermede een Javaens Inwoonder van Anjer, met een advijs briefje geschreven op gisteren door den Coopman Colijn, en den Schipper van het schip dieren Iacob Coel, dat toe VHo Ed speculatie in originele bij desen p. r Expresse vlieger Van Bantam den 27:' Maart 1693. voortgaet, en om desen niet op te houden, ons eerbiedig aen sullen gedragen, en eenlijk Seggen, als dat de Andromeda, wie op den 17. ' deser, alhier ter rhede is aengeland, vermits de paesdagen eerst op eergisteren morgen, na het Eijland panjang, met voorkennisse vanden Sultan, om de aldaer in gereetheijt zijnde 500. moten kamhout, in te nemen, is verseijlt, van waer wij hem ten spoedigsten wederom te gemoet zien, om voorts de souten met harpuijs te vullen, en verders 't gene van dat Barst bij de pakhuijsen berust ingenomen hebbende, die bodem voorts met peper inder spoed sonder tijd versuijm sal volgen. Waermede &. a onderston en was getekent Edmunt van sterrevelt, willem kaeff, W: kuffeler, G: Pietersen, en Zacharias Rooman, ter Sijden stond Bantam 27. n Mart 1693. en daer onderstont P: S: het briefje uijt het schip dieren, aen uEd: gesz: volgens luijt vant hier inleggende briefje, is hier nog niet aengebragt.
text_translated_detailed: received on the 30th of March 1643 [uncertain: likely 1693]. by native vessel Bantacco on the 27th of March 1693. From Batavia to the well-esteemed Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies, Your Honour's high and esteemed [authority], Earnest, great esteemed, Valiant, wise, aforementioned, most generous and well-mannered gentlemen. Well-esteemed, strict Gentlemen. After this morning the small ship the pepper arrived here at the roadstead and brought ashore Your Honour's high and esteemed well-valued missive, signed by the Esteemed Mister Secretary Paulus de Roo, dated the 25th current, so hereby appears a Javanese inhabitant of Anjer, with an advisory letter written yesterday by the merchant Colijn, and the skipper of the ship Dieren [modern equivalent: ship name] Jacob Coel, which for Your Honour's consideration in original herewith proceeds by express messenger. From Bantam on the 27th of March 1693. and in order not to delay this, we shall conduct ourselves respectfully, and only say, that the Andromeda, which arrived here at the roadstead on the 17th of this month, since the Easter days only the day before yesterday morning, toward the island Panjang, with the foreknowledge of the Sultan, to take on the 500 masts of kamwood [uncertain: type of wood] that were in readiness there, has sailed, from where we expect to meet him again as soon as possible, in order to proceed to fill the holds with pepper using harping, and further what from that Barst [uncertain: possibly a ship or location] rests at the warehouses having taken in, that vessel shall proceed with pepper in haste without time delay. Wherewith &c. stood and was signed Edmund van Stervelt, Willem Kaeff, W: Kuffeler, G: Pietersen, and Zacharias Rooman, beside stood Bantam 27th of March 1693. and there stood P.S.: the letter from the ship Dieren, to Your Honour's aforementioned [attention], according to the contents of the letter herein enclosed, has not yet been brought here.

text_translated_detailed: Received 3 April 1643. — By a Javanese vessel from Bantam on the 28th of March 1698. — Batavia to the Esteemed and Honored Lord M. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and Esteemed and Honored Lords, Councillors of the Netherlands India, Your Esteemed Excellencies, Most Earnest, Wise, Aforementioned, Most Esteemed and Generous Lords, Your Esteemed and Strict Excellencies. The letter herein conveyed to Your Esteemed Excellency by the officers of the ship Dieren, subscribed by them, and which was sent hither by their Excellencies with the accompanying letter of introduction, shall make known that the vessel on the 26th of this month was at the side of the fourth corner, having only been stationed here yesterday, since the fishermen, notwithstanding that they are seven men strong, were unable to haul it up from under the shore due to the fierce currents, the tide still running out, which we hope will change with the new moon, and then turn, the wind in their favor from Bantam on the 28th of March 1693 shall also blow through so that sooner they may drop their anchor at the desired roadstead there, and the officers may appear before Your Esteemed Excellency, since the Andromeda, through the violent rolling of the sea and the fierce burnings, has until now been able to obtain no more than 150 nutmeg trees; the hard burnings likewise will not cease, according to appearances, before the new moon, so the officers of that vessel have resolved to command 250 nutmeg trees to be taken in, to come hither, for his pepper cargo, and then the pepper garden so as not to lose any time, so that 2 to 300 nutmeg trees shall sail to the Island Panjang, which are to be fetched from there, so that that garden, likewise fully laden with pepper, with all speed and without loss of time shall be brought to the roadstead there, standing in quantity and quality of the aforementioned goods, each to carry half, no time

text_translated_detailed: Received by inland transport on the 30th of May 1693. From Bantam on the 3rd of May 1693—Recently departed from Bengal, those same vessels had advanced yesterday evening near the Cannibal Island [uncertain: "mensch Eters Eijland"], where they were held up by the continuous northeast winds and opposing currents. The provisions sent to them consisted of double portions, since both those vessels were patrimonial ships of the Company, which was all the more necessary due to the great number of invalids. For this reason we trust that our action will be regarded as well done, with which &c. [abbreviated: et cetera] was signed and undersigned Edmund van Sterrevelt, at Bantam on the 3rd of May 1693.—To Batavia, to the well-esteemed Mister M. [Mijnheer] Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Indies of the Netherlands, His Excellency's most earnest, great, mighty, valiant, wise, aforementioned, generous Gentlemen, His Excellency's commanding Gentlemen. This reaches your Excellency accompanied by a Missive from Bantam of the 26th of May 1693, which has been brought here today by express messenger by way of the sea, and has been subscribed to your Excellency by the officers of the ship Goudesteijn [ship name], to which I have attached an authentic copy of the letter sent by the same person hither, the ship Langewijk already being in our sight, making all efforts to gain the voyage to your Excellency. And since tomorrow our lengthy writings, with a certain legal process here in the Council of Justice, are required regarding and against a slave of the deceased Colonel Jan Fransen, who here has been declared mad and deprived of his senses, to whom he has given over the gambling, and attempted to escape the deeds he could commit; so this shall now serve solely as an accompaniment to the aforementioned missive, with which &c. was signed and undersigned Edmund van Sterrevelt, W. Kuffeler, G. Pietersen, G. Wijs, and Z. Hooman. At the side it states Bantam on the 26th and May 1643. Batavia.

Received at Batavia on the 1st of June 1693 by the Mardyker [a mixed-race community] Candese. From Bantam on the 30th of May 1693. Most earnest, great, mighty, valiant, wise, aforementioned, most generous Gentlemen. The Almighty is beseeched to ward off all plagues from us, and to mitigate the great damage that the Chinese have suffered in this fire; since we see no opportunity to be able to bring the Elephant of Bantam on board, inasmuch as there is no plank laid over the streams and it will not step, much less will it be able to be brought to stand in the boat with constructed platforms. text_translated_detailed: From Bantam on the 13th of June 1693. To Batavia, to the Honorable and Esteemed Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India. Honorable and Esteemed, Most Serious, Great and Worthy, Wise, and Most Generous Gentlemen. To the Pangeran Nattor diradja we have on the night before last made known to Your Honorable Excellency, as last mentioned, and with due respect reported, that to the realm's administrator 17,000 rixdollars [rd.s] had been allocated, of which the Sultan has disbursed 7,000, for the payment of the pepper received, and the remainder has been placed in the court treasury, likewise the other pepper traders have been put off until such time as Your Honorable Excellency shall be pleased to send cash again, and so that the Sultan would have that pretext, the pepper sharpening, which the Javanese now and then delay, through the withholding of straw sacks, by which it has been prevented that eleven vessels have not yet unloaded and have remained lying, such a foolish situation has come about, whose unloading and the obtaining of the sacks now stands to take better progress. Before the end of this month we intend to have in the Company's warehouses 3,000 bales of well-sharpened and pure pepper, of which already 1,525 bales have been transferred to the Company's warehouses, by the dispatch held with the realm's administrator two days ago, which now departs, so as not to hold up the ship any longer, because the dispatch has remained unsealed, since the realm's administrator's desire was that a greater quantity of pepper should be received before the final dispatch and brought into that dispatch. Upon the second movement of the earth, the sea swelled very high three times. From Bantam on the 15th of June 1693. over the land, struck much, many families and cattle thereby perished and torn away. Two islands lying thereabout were inundated, and which would have disappeared. All the vessels of both aforementioned places standing on the shore were smashed to pieces and swept away by the river, as by seawater. Having on the previous Friday in the afternoon here again felt the earthquake, which God be thanked was very slight. After the closing of our respectful last writing, Abdul van Boegis Castle, alias Tampoerna van Biema, slave of the Carpenter Pieter Ferera, who dwells there outside the Rotterdam gate, on the road from Anthiol, who was brought in chains to the yacht the Castle Batavia, had been detained here as far as Ceram over the w. months. The same one, who against the amok player Company of Toroeja, in the Council of Justice was confronted, and no guilt could be found in him, was sent there, in order that his master might procure his release, by paying the ordinary maintenance costs, ransom, and the expenses incurred thereupon, to the sum of 14. rd. s which the General Office shall subsequently be charged with. From Bantam on the 15th of June 1693.

text_translated_detailed: Received on the 10th of July 1693, by the Chaloupe [small boat] the Castle Batavia. From Bantam on the 8th of July 1693. Batavia. To the Honored, Esteemed, Most Wise, Foresaid, Most Generous Gentlemen, the Honored Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Your Honors' Most Esteemed, Most Steadfast, Most Valiant, Most Wise, Aforesaid, Most Generous Gentlemen. Your Honors' Well-Esteemed Letters of the 18th and 20th of the previous month have been duly received here on the 19th and 21st respectively, with the jacht [small ship] the Castle Batavia, as well as by the Sultan's Contingent, through the Pangeran Natta Diradja, and upon which with all due respect and diligence, the three chests, or the 15,000 pieces of silver reales, were unloaded from the aforementioned jacht on the first-mentioned day, and the following day, by Captain Lieutenant Willem Kuffelaer and Lieutenant Gerrit Pietersen, in the presence of the Governor and with the attendance of the chief steersman Lieve Bek and the bookkeeper Joost van de Rondewerken, were counted and found to be 2½ reales short, which were previously supplied, and on the 22nd were handed over to the treasurer, amounting to ƒ44,500, for which the General Office shall be credited. text_translated_detailed: The Sultan has been pleased to burden [the Company] with a request from the Governor, with the express condition that His Highness might obtain it in due course. However, since the packages of considerable Tapechindos [uncertain: possibly a type of cloth or goods] were refused by the Sultan, the Governor requested to be accommodated with them instead. Although the Commander found himself somewhat constrained in this matter, yet relying on the hope that Your Honors would view this favorably and that he would not have consented to anything improper, the Governor proceeded accordingly and obtained two packages of these goods at Bantam's own request, in the hope that Your Honors will be pleased to regard this favorably. Since the aforementioned His Excellency will pay this to the Company's Treasury with 280 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] in cash, without prejudice to His Excellency's request made to Your High Honors beforehand, all the more so since his allegation is to accommodate the Lamponders [residents of Lampung] in their request. From Bantam, the 18th of July 1693. And if this is indeed the case and cannot be construed too much to his advantage, it is of lesser importance, and the Commander's request—His Excellency's dispensation regarding this—Your High Honors will be pleased to send in good order. When he comes to learn that his request has been granted, he shall then send there. This message was brought to the Governor by the Kiai Aria Iaja Sedana, who reported that in Batavia some information had been heard regarding such timber work, but he had not been able to find it, so with respect to the needs of Sultan Timme. Bantam the 30th of August 1693. From necessity compelled, Your Honour with this request to trouble you. On this occasion we find ourselves obliged to advise that for the past three days seven vessels have arrived here from Lampon Poeti with 280 bales of black old, or over-year-old pepper, which the Governor shall cause to be unloaded as quickly as possible, so that whatever may have become wet among the vessels may be dried by the sun and air before being taken to the warehouse, so that it may be admitted for further inspection, and after being winnowed 3 or 4 times, or as often as necessary, it shall be received by the King's scribes, and then subsequently in due time here within the Company's warehouses shall be stored.
