Upon receipt of Your Honor's letter, the bookkeepers Joost van de Ronde Werken and Matthijs Andries Route were appointed as commissioners, to winnow the pepper lying here in the warehouse once more, with the order to perform that work with good attention and speed, and if necessary, the rightful [authority] from Bantam on the 21st of September 1693, of their actions with oath may declare, just as for this fourth winnowing 100 sacks, brought from the warehouse onto the scale weighing 7560 pounds, which by the aforementioned commissioners were winnowed, were found to weigh 7454 pounds, thus in underweight, and through the winnowing fell 106 pounds of husk and dust of pepper, making 1 3/8 [modern equivalent: approximately 1.4 percent] underweight. This is not worthy of the attention of Your High Honors in this matter, but I advised the Captain that it would be best if he came to reconcile with Lord Sterrevelt, and that all those trifles through which the disagreement between them both had arisen should be mortified [set aside], and that henceforth he come to better understanding with the other, and live in peace and tranquility. For both must be assured that if the disagreement comes before Your Honors, it will appear entirely unpleasant, but very soon thereafter they must expect nothing other than to be sharply reproached, and also that one of both will then have to move away. The Captain showed himself entirely inclined toward reconciliation, but between them both, an intermediary will be needed for this to happen well. His Excellency promised to do my utmost regarding Lord Sterrevelt, and I trust nothing else but that this Lord will allow himself to be found amenable. Meanwhile, some courtiers came to visit the Captain, and related how Radin Mandaraka, younger brother of Pangeran Purbaya, had suffered a sudden stroke yesterday, at Bantam on the 19th of April 1693. — and two hours thereafter came to die, leaving behind two legitimate wives and three children, which Pangeran Joukia has taken under his protection. The eldest wife is a daughter of Pangeran Kulan, and the other is a granddaughter of Pangeran Diapa Ningrat.

text_translated_detailed: the day before yesterday concerning his Majesty. It was in Bantam on the 19th of April 1693. He had communicated what had previously occurred, and that now everything was well, hoping that payment to the pepper traders would henceforth be made at the proper time. The King intends to send one of his trusted heads of the Sura Nagaras [administrative districts], named Tsiacra Nagara, with 30 to 40 men into the mountains to search more thoroughly for a fugitive Calang, whom they have been seeking for some time already from others, and from whom they have been unable to obtain the slightest news. He has special orders that, after he has done his duty everywhere in the mountains and villages, whether he finds the said fugitive Calang or not, he should set his course over Tangerang to Batavia in order to report this to Your Honour there, and that when I arrive in Batavia, I would make this known, and that his Majesty for this time had nothing more to command, and with this, after the Pangerang had once again recommended his humble greetings to Your Honour, I took my leave. In the evening we received our farewell from the Honourable Governor van Sterrevelt, and we thereupon immediately boarded the small vessel the Andromeda, and with daybreak began our return journey, on which we were so delayed by severe contrary winds and strong currents that we have not been able until today to discharge our humble duty to Your Honour. With which &c. was signed W. Caeff, at Batavia on the 19th of April 1693.

text_translated_detailed: Received in Batavia 4th October 1693. P.r Dearias Iaja Sedana and Soeta Widsjastra. From Bantam on the 2nd of October 1693. Batavia. To the Honourable and Esteemed Mister M.r Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India. Honourable and Esteemed, Most Worthy, Wise aforementioned, and most generous Gentlemen. Honourable and Esteemed Gentlemen, on the 25th of the past month, the ship Bantam arrived here at the roadstead, after which the Honourable Rijxbestierder [chief administrator] Natta Widjaja appeared within the anchorage, announcing in the name of the Sultan that the Majesty intended to have Your Honour's esteemed letter and the gift for the young Prince Pangeran Ratoe brought ashore with all honours. Thereupon the Governor, in order to give the Gentlemen Commissioners notice thereof, prepared a letter, and before the same could be sent, the Gentlemen Commissioners learned upon coming ashore that Your Honour's esteemed letter, dated the 23rd of the past month, had been delivered to us. When the Governor communicated the Sultan's intention to them, they deemed it good to make known to the Honourable Rijxbestierder that the Honourable Commissioners would be aboard on behalf thereof to await the Sultan's Patchall [official delegation] there, and to see the Commissioners of the King meet them there, as they did the next morning; transported by means of; followed by the Honourable Cufflaer [official], and the Fiscal Guiljam Wijs, and likewise with the tide the Sultan's Commissioners Pangeran Narta Widjaja, the Ken Aria Singa Meroeda, together with various Kingabeijs [nobles] and Tommogons [officials], who in the afternoon came ashore under the firing of nine cannon shots from the ship and subsequently in the afternoon came to land, also bringing Your Honour's esteemed letter in a silver dish, and all the goods belonging to the gift, which were brought in proper order within the anchorage under honours.

Honourable and Esteemed Gentlemen, on the 25th of the past month, the ship Bantam arrived here at the roadstead, after which the Honourable Rijxbestierder chief administrator Natta Widjaja appeared within the anchorage, announcing in the name of the Sultan that the Majesty intended to have Your Honour's esteemed letter and the gift for the young Prince Pangeran Ratoe brought ashore with all honours. Thereupon the Governor, in order to give the Gentlemen Commissioners notice thereof, prepared a letter, and before the same could be sent, the Gentlemen Commissioners learned upon coming ashore that Your Honour's esteemed letter, dated the 23rd of the past month, had been delivered to us. When the Governor communicated the Sultan's intention to them, they deemed it good to make known to the Honourable Rijxbestierder that the Honourable Commissioners would be aboard on behalf thereof to await the Sultan's Patchall official delegation there, and to see the Commissioners of the King meet them there, as they did the next morning; transported by means of; followed by the Honourable Cufflaer official, and the Fiscal Guiljam Wijs, and likewise with the tide the Sultan's Commissioners Pangeran Narta Widjaja, the Ken Aria Singa Meroeda, together with various Kingabeijs nobles and Tommogons officials, who in the afternoon came ashore under the firing of nine cannon shots from the ship and subsequently in the afternoon came to land, also bringing Your Honour's esteemed letter in a silver dish, and all the goods belonging to the gift, which were brought in proper order within the anchorage under honours.

text_translated_detailed: confirmed in his father's place, who likewise until his death enjoyed the same goodness of the Dutch Company. After him his brother the Paduca Sirij Sultan, Aboe Lamahasin Mahomet Zien Noel Abidien, was crowned to the succession as King in the realm of Bantam, to whom the Governor General and the Councillors of India now at this time show ever more and more their willing help and support, as their Honour Excellency at that time, for that purpose, also with an upright intention, had the goodness to send a gentleman from the midst of their assembly to Sourosoan to deliberate upon everything that was serviceable to the welfare of the realm with the great Mantris and lesser Pongawas, who then completed this work according to the old custom without the least alteration, and followed the unbreakable right of the Kings — such that it shall never depart from our thoughts, much less that we would forget it, but on the contrary we shall always remain obliged to the Dutch Company for it. We have also read that it was very pleasing to Your Excellency to hear that the Sultan had established good order for the speedy payment made to the merchants who bring their pepper to Sourosoan. All this the Sultan did not do of himself, but this happened through the good instruction of Your Excellency from Bantam under date of the 26th of October 1693, which provides us with the means and first sends ready money for the payment to Sourosoan, whereby the merchants shall also be encouraged, as the brought pepper is paid to the satisfaction of the suppliers. How well pleased with Your Excellency's Honour we have seen from the manifold blessings and good wishes bestowed upon us with our young son, who must also be raised according to the manner of the King's children, so that no worldly discomforts may befall him,

text_translated_detailed: and when some stones had been broken out from there, we found them so firmly mortared that, whatever effort and care might be expended, very few whole stones can be obtained from there, or will be able to be obtained, besides which the wages of the coolies [laborers] who are employed for that purpose would come to amount to more than the stones that would come out of there are worth. Up to now no stone arch, threshold, or clinker stones have been discovered, notwithstanding that the upper floor, being made of heads, is already two stones deep laid, and in order to make the excavation deeper for the discovery of threshold or clinker stones, one has not dared to proceed, for fear that through too much disturbance of the foundation, one might easily cause a collapse of the upper structure. Besides this, the Governor of Bantam on the 10th of November 1693 has found inches on the sides of the inner door to have been set in square coral stone, for which reason we have deemed it fitting to let the filling of the cellar proceed further, without expending any further effort on the breaking out of stones. The Sultan and the realm's administrator, upon our request, have consented that we may fetch and take the earth needed for filling the cellar from the place where some heights will present themselves to us, all of which we hope with Your Honored Excellence's good pleasure will have been agreed upon. The fugitive slave woman Costoerij, of whom mention was made in our humble letters sent on the 26th of last month, was to be transported by the King's vessels from here to Batavia, and on the 31st of last month was sent under the supervision of the keij [official] Ingabeij Elaxa Diprana. In the aforementioned letters of ours we forgot to ask Your Honored Excellence to note that the Sultan on the 8th of October was again blessed with the birth of a young son, obtained from one of his concubines.

text_translated_detailed: Keij Aria Iaja Sedana communicated that the Captain of the Chinese here, Swasinko, upon his departure to Batavia had left here to oversee his affairs, and the King's income, with him leased, the Chinese Swateke, and that since the aforementioned Captain recently died in Batavia, and the last-mentioned Chinese, the King in the oversight of the taken-over affairs of the aforementioned deceased Captain had granted satisfaction, His Majesty would gladly see that the aforementioned Swa Teenko be appointed again as head of the Chinese here, if that could be agreed upon with Your Honorable Excellency's good consent; the aforementioned Tommegon also having orders to inquire further regarding the Sultan's affection in this respect and to explain it by word of mouth to Your Honorable Excellency, and if there should be a light brown or indeed black Burmese horse in the Company's stables, to request that for His Majesty from Your Honorable Excellency, to make a saddle-horse [telenaer: a type of riding horse] for his Queen, but if no such horse should be in the stables, then with Your Excellency's permission he might go search for one in the city, and upon obtaining such a horse, purchase it and bring it here, the Sultan having returned from this place in the night of his pleasure journey from Bantam the 6th of December 1693, since the indisposition of the Pangeran Ratoe, which is now somewhat improving, had only been His Majesty's concern up to a certain point; text_translated_detailed: Received the 12th of December 1693 by the Patchall the Sea Hare. Bantam 11th of December 1693. — From Batavia, from the well-esteemed Mister M. W. van Outhoorn, Governor General and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India. Esteemed, most worthy, courageous, wise, aforementioned, and very generous Gentlemen. On the 9th of this month the Patchall the Sea Hare arrived here with Your Honorable Excellency's letters of the 6th written previously, and the next day the Jaggie [expanded: Jaggie, a type of vessel] the Snaeuw [normalized: the Snow], with Your Honorable Excellency's writings of the 7th mentioned, regarding which we respectfully say that upon seeing the return fleet yesterday preparations were made for sending the ordered livestock, but the fallen rain yesterday and the low water were the cause that we could not send the same any earlier than this morning, consisting of 26 pieces of well-conditioned cattle. As was notified to us by the Commander of the return fleet yesterday evening, the ship with Your Honorable Excellency's papers also came in the fleet, lying anchored just around the corner of Bantam. In accordance with Your Honorable Excellency's order, now departs with the aforementioned Patchall also to Batavia, the Lieutenant Gerrit Pietersen, with his family. With the loading of the Jaggie the Snaeuw, from Bantam the 11th of December 1693, a beginning shall be made tomorrow, and as soon as the ship of the King of Bantam arrives at this roadstead, the stock of pepper at the Company's warehouses shall be unloaded into it at the earliest, consisting of 690 bundles of pure harped black pepper, and then at once we shall make known how much pepper by estimation can be ready against Your Excellency's order of this month. With which [signature] was signed, Willem Caeff, Willem Sabelaer and Zacharias Rooman, on the side it states Bantam 11th of December 1643. — Batavia. To his Excellency Master W. van Outhoorn, Governor General, and Esteemed Gentlemen

text_translated_detailed: From Bantam 15th December 1693. Batavia From the Honored Mister M. W. van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honored Gentlemen Councilors of the Netherlands Indies Honored, Esteemed, High Lordship, valiant, per the Yacht the Snauw received 17th December 1693. As aforesaid: very generous, strong on the 11th of this month in the morning our last respectful letters to Your High Honor departed, per the Patchall the Zeehase, in the hands of Lieutenant Gerant Pietersen, on which day in the afternoon, there also arrived here the Yacht the King of Bantam, which, being already busy loading, is to return within two or three days with as much pepper as is stored at the warehouses of the Honored Company and the King, amounting to approximately 8 to 400 bales, and that after the completion of that yacht, then no noteworthy quantity of that grain will remain to be given to the fluyt Nierop from the Prince's Island standing here, but because Your High Honor would gladly be served from here at the earliest with 25 to 30 Coijangs [uncertain: type of vessel or measure] of suitable salt, and the Yacht the Snauw was sent expressly to fetch that salt, but 16 Javanese Coijangs could be taken, which per the first invoice is to be charged, and with which that small vessel Batavia-ward steers, so we have Your Honor deemed it well to approve, per the Yacht the Company's of Bantam received 19th December 1693. text_translated_detailed: From Bantam on the 5th of January 1694. — From the 25th thereof, with the safe arrival of the Chialoep [small vessel] Padang, it has gone well, and with the Chialoep we have received Lieutenant Jan Gerard van der Plasse and the 25 common soldiers, specified in the accompanying name roll of those who arrived, the said Lieutenant being placed in the position of the departed Lieutenant Gerrit Pietersz, stationed in Speelwijk, and the other soldiers distributed to the posts in accordance with Your Honour's orders. They go with the Chialoep now back to Batavia. Of the further released soldiers, 25 persons according to the attached name roll, and among them three sergeants, with the departure of which so many posts in the Castle Diamond and Speelwijk are left without sergeants, over which the supervision has been deferred to three of the most capable Corporals, until such time as Your Honour shall again provide us with other sergeants in place of those now departing. And on Carangomontoe on the 12th of December of the past year deceased, and of which Your Honour was given notice on the 16th thereof, you will be pleased to see, or find it good that those Corporals be appointed as sergeants for the time being. Going besides the aforementioned released persons, there also goes over the summoned soldier Barent Cramer from Amsterdam, and here beside for Your Honour's consideration a brief account of the military forces present here and where they are stationed. Moreover, this is accompanied by a name roll of various soldiers from Bantam on the 5th of January 1694, whose time has well expired, as will be evident thereby, whom we with their behalf from Your Honour's respectfully request such improvement of wages as is mentioned by each one's name, being therewith established Erasmus Labrasf from Amsterdam in the year 1690 on the 11th of August by Your Honour taken into service as a sailor with ƒ 8 per month [modern equivalent: guilders per month] under a three-year contract, and on the 18th of December

text_translated_detailed: prowa Sedana, with our escort letters from the 6th of December, departed for Batavia, returned on the 22nd thereof, with a note as he has reported to us from Your Honour to the Company, whereby the regent of the realm on the same day has let us know that Your Honour would have written, upon the proposal and request of His Majesty, the Chinese Swateenko, to have been appointed as Captain or chief over the Chinese Nation here, in place of the deceased Captain Swasianco at Batavia. The mentioned Chinese Swateenko meanwhile went to Batavia once more for a time, and having returned again on the 28th of December, has also communicated to us through Your Honour that he has been appointed as chief over his nation here, and there by His Excellency, the Governor General himself, has been wished good fortune therewith. Since when the King, whether from his own inclination or through the advice of the aforementioned Swateenko (unknown to us for now), has undertaken and decided to have this Chinese presented here on a Monday the 4th of this month, in the manner as the deceased Captain Swasiamko was presented, which has been communicated to us in the name of the King and regent of the realm through the Kiai Aria Jaya Sedana on the 31st of the past month. But we, being without Your Honour's approval and order in that regard and foreseen, let it serve as an answer thereupon that Your Honour had not been pleased to give us notice of that appointment, and we therefore considering ourselves incompetent, because without Your Honour's order the Company's behalf, here from Bantam on the 5th of January 1694, to do so, with the request that if it please His Majesty, the desired presentation might be postponed for another 6 to 8 days, doubting whether, since Your Honour had written to His Majesty upon his request to have appointed this Chinese as Captain, Your Honour would at the first opportunity also give us notice thereof

From Bantam on the 5th of January 163 for that purpose; brought in by a keij aria in a silver dish expressly for this, with the recommendation of the Sultan's representative to be pleased to put on and use it. We now humbly request that Your Honour not take amiss our actions for the reasons alleged, and we shall herewith conclude. text_translated_detailed: From Bantam dated the 18th of January 1694. On this day, the 15th of January 1694, there appeared before me Francois Mesnagie, first clerk of this secretariat, and by the chief merchant and governor Edmund van Sterrevelt and council qualified to make all manner of public acts and instruments, present the aforementioned witnesses Joost vande rondewerken, bookkeeper in the service of the Company and here within the fort described, declared at the request of the esteemed commissioned merchants W. Caef and W. Sabelaer, to be true and truthful, that in the month of April of the previous year 1693, there had come to this roadstead the ship the perthuijn, being the governor's vessel, in order to be loaded with pepper. And having received one or two vessels according to his proper orders from the warehouses within the fort, which were then emptied, the governor charged the assistant Hartman vander klump to harp the pepper with the most recently arrived vessel at once, and to unload it into the aforementioned small ship. Whereupon the said Hartman vander klump replied to His Excellency that the pepper was still damp and entirely unsuitable to pass over the harping apparatus. So His Excellency the governor had me, the attestant, called to him, and showed a small sample of the newly brought pepper and asked, what do you think of the pepper? To which the attestant replied, according to the sample, in his judgment that pepper seemed good. From Bantam dated the 18th of January 1601, the governor added thereto: "Eh, sire, who says that pepper is not good?" Ordering His Excellency the attestant to transport with the pepper-lading assistant Jacob Willemsen to the King's Harping House, and to harp the aforementioned pepper, which was also followed by us. But we found when harping that this grain was so damp, just as the aforementioned Hartman vander klump had previously made known to the governor.

Furthermore I declare, the deponent, 2 to 3 days after the date, was told by the Honourable commander aforementioned to be used henceforth for pepper drying, and each time to show the pepper to the commander, when he himself would judge, and I the deponent had only to dry, which I have strictly carried out.

text_translated_detailed: From Bantam dated 18 January 1694, I received [a letter] which does not please me well, and you do my will if you do well, just as on 4 June of this month I have had [pepper] winnowed 9 to 10 times, consisting of 1932 sacks, of which the longest [batches] lay 3 to 4 days, two times one day on land, and one time as soon as the sacks were filled, [they were] brought to the winnowing machine and winnowed, against which the Javanese scribes opposed me, saying that such was not customary, whereupon I asked them to have the Honored Superintendent attend to this, since [I was] attending [to it] daily and each time received bad answers, and did not dare speak anymore, because once and for all it had been recommended [to me] to follow His Honor's orders without contradiction, further not declaring anything other than what was mentioned above, [which I] pretend to [maintain] at all times, and being asked to do so with solemn oath, [I] confirmed the same further. thus done and attested in the city of Bantam, within the Company's palisade Speelwijk, on the day, month and year mentioned above in the presence of Marijn Andriesen Route and Andries Baentsz. Barents Appeldoorn, both bookkeepers in the service of the Honored Company, as witnesses requested here, who have signed the original of this together with the Declarant and me, first Clerk. Undersigned in my knowledge was signed F. Nesnage. Batavia. text_translated_detailed: New India by express courier received on 20 January 1694. From Bantam on 21 January 1694. Esteemed, Honored, Wise, Aforementioned and Very Generous Gentlemen. These few lines are principally directed as an accompaniment to the enclosed Letter herein, which has just come to us from the Strait of Sunda from the ship the King William, together with which to Your Honored Esteemed consideration the original has been handed over, the note by the head merchant Gerardus Altorfius, under yesterday's date to the Honored Superintendent Edmund van Stervelt, etc., together with a cold [inventory] list of the servants present on that vessel in being, etc., the unwinnowed hundred [bales] of pepper, of which in our respectful Letters by the sloop yesterday to Your Honored Esteemed [was] sent, [has] today been inspected and [they] have been found suitable and dry enough to be received as winnowed, which then could also happen tomorrow morning, the yacht the Steadfastness from here will carry over 500 bales of that [pepper], and within 2 to 3 days turn the bow toward Batavia, with which, etc., [it] was understood and was signed Edmund van Stervelt, E. Creff, W. Sabelaer, G. Wijs and Z. Roman, at the side stood Bantam on 21 January 1644 [sic]. Batavia. To the Honored, Esteemed Mister W. van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of New India.

text_translated_detailed: Received 28 January 1694. Wise, Aforementioned, Very Generous Gentlemen. On the 14th of this month in the evening our last respectful letters to Your Honored Esteemed went out by express courier, as accompaniment to a sealed letter from the ship the King William, arrived from the Fatherland in the Strait of Sunda, received, whose receipt we hope. Of the winnowing equipment, by the royal administrator there is still in stock approximately 400 pounds, of which gum we could well have shipped a greater quantity, than considering Your Honored Esteemed will gladly [understand], the sooner the better it would be with the pepper, for the ready-lying return ships, and to ship a greater quantity of that gum would still require two to three days, as [it] must first be sought out, so it is best judged that this vessel, without further time loss, should depart with the already taken winnowing equipment. text_translated_detailed: being in a state to make a voyage to Batavia with this vessel for the purpose of conducting his examination, it will please Your Honour, as soon as conditions improve, to follow the first opportunity. The three Dutch flat-bottomed boats per the Chialdep Padang from Bantam on the 21st of January 1694, brought from Batavia on the 25th of October last, have not been placed on the Sultan's most recently closed account because the realm's administrator, in the Sultan's name, had caused it to be declared that those should first, and until those four rolls per the ship Bantam on the 25th of September, for His Majesty's account be brought, be consumed, might remain stored at the Company's warehouses, as soon as His Majesty is pleased to have them received, they shall be entered into his account. The Moor Mamenina, since the departure of our letter of the 10th of this month, the value of approximately only 20 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch silver coins] in clothing, has handed over to us, and having declared that he could find no other or greater goods for his and his companion Abdul Kadier's account, nor any outstanding debts, those clothes now go per this vessel to Your Honour, having been packed in a package by express appointed commissioners, and thus delivered to the ship's authority, namely L.A., and of which clothes a further memorandum, accompanying this, shall be sent. The aforementioned Mamenina per inland vessel, according to his statement, shall depart the day after tomorrow also to Batavia, in order to give his companion further explanation by word of mouth concerning their outstanding matters here. The Sultan has caused us to be informed that he is in need of 200 Dutch kiate planks [uncertain: specific type of wooden plank], and requests that these be procured by Your Honour and sent together with the previously procured green cloth at the first opportunity, which we, by this, humbly do.

text_translated_detailed: Imbanagara came here to us, whose timber works we also paid, just as we then also spoke further with him, regarding his request concerning VHo[nor]Ed[dresses]: agtb[?]: concerning the villages Pamotang and Passourouang done, and he himself acknowledged that Rapa Mangala the administration of Pamotang and Rassa Banegfa of Passourouan, the same from fathers to fathers have had, there him on served, that he then well could make a stand, since he as well as the other prianger[s] heads, under the Comp[any]'s obedience stood, that they with gladness under him the party or someone else would be inclined to submit, just as then trust he the party, also not gladly under the Pangeram of Samadang or anyone else would want to stand, thereby adding that the Comp[any]'s government with that From Cirebon [Sirbon:] the 9th of March 1693. — of the Sousouh[?]. entirely different was, that the Javanese customs were, to take from one another his own, but that the Comp[any] such not desired, but that each one his own in peace and without being troubled would possess, and since your Ho[nor]Ed[dresses]: besides, the hands sufficiently occupied have, not gladly with unnecessary and unfounded pretensions troubled are and regarding his people, over which he himself, at your Ed[dresses]: Ho[nor]: agtb[?].— complained, that he in proportion of 1000. men to the Comp[any]'s timber-cutting contributes, there he effectively but 700. men possesses, thereupon have we served him that he henceforth but for 700. men to contribute had, and then it his own free will been is, that he thus long in proportion of 1000. men given has, to the end to draw equal share beside the other heads, he pleased himself in the first very well to be satisfied, that henceforth but pro rata of 700. men would contribute, From Cirebon [Sirbon:] the 9th of March 1693.

text_translated_detailed: Wouter Kleijnman, after sending [to] the Priangan lands to have the Company's timber works that lay ready there brought together, and to send [them] to Indramaju, so that we, as soon as Van Tirbon on the 9th of March 1693 — at least as soon as possible with the unloading of the salt fleets we may make a beginning, of which now already 10 frames are again in readiness and properly joined together. 120 pounds of pepper, 2000 sticks of whole barrel staves, 100 pieces of small house beams, long 2 to 23 feet and thick 6 to 7 inches [modern equivalent: approximately 0.6-7 meters long and 15-18 centimeters thick] we have here in readiness with us, according to the aforementioned esteemed notification. With which &c. undersigned Isaac Ringh, Elias Vredenhoff and was signed and Lucas Munster, beside whom stood Sirbon in the fort the Protection on the 9th of March 1693:— and thereunder E: E: High Esteemed Gentlemen, since the daily violent storm and rainy weather, so there has been no one who has dared to choose the sea, which is the reason that this now has not made progress, which we hope Your Esteemed will not take amiss, the Lieutenant Engineer Bajonville arrived here on the 17th of this month from Japara with the patchall [uncertain: type of vessel] the Lily; which after some few repairs and refreshment as now the journey according to Your Esteemed Van Tirbon on the 29th of March 1693 — proceeds without anything further having occurred here, except only the Soldier Daniel van Kalker, who here on the 16th of this month toward evening came to pass away, whom we the following day had committed to the earth. With which E: undersigned and was signed Isaac Ringh. Beside whom stood Sirbon on the 19th of March 1693.— Batavia To the High Esteemed Mister Willem van Outhoorn Governor General and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India High Esteemed, great respect, Manly, wise, aforesaid.

text_translated_detailed: Resident Ring returned here on the 30th from Indermaijo, having previously sent from there his very humble letter of the 23rd of May to Your Honour, in which it was mentioned, among other things, how they were preparing to send six named vessels to sea, each loaded with a cargo of beams, which has since been done, and with which Sergeant Hosmeester and the Carpenters are now busy loading further, so that it is hoped these will be ready around the middle of this month to be able to undertake the journey to Batavia. Just as the Jagje de Sint Nicolaes is now also returning from Sirbon on the 2nd of June 1693 to Your Honour with 2541½ pounds of black pepper, net 2600 pounds, whole wooden planks 100 pounds, small house beams. According to the enclosed bill of lading and invoice, Your Honour will humbly be shown, amounting to a sum of ƒ4162.15.-. For this we shall properly debit the general office with Your Honour's permission, with this opportunity of the now departing Jagje we have deemed it good to relieve ourselves of the prisoners here, who now go to Your Honour, so that the name roll herewith attached will humbly show Your Honour, trusting that this will not be disagreeable to Your Honour. As nothing particularly noteworthy has occurred here otherwise, except that our chief surgeon Jan Hendrik Bontos, after a long lingering illness, passed away on the 27th of the recently passed month, whom we have, according to time and place, decently buried. From Sirbon on the 2nd of June 1693. We therefore very humbly request that with Your Honour's convenience and pleasure we may be provided with another good master in his place. The testament of the deceased, whereby his estate is bequeathed to his natural child and its mother, being a Balinese woman.

The debt of Keij Oina Marta Nata to Sultan Anum has been presented for payment several times, but he now sings again his old tune of wanting 2000 rixdollars yearly, which we were still pressed about today, so that we cannot sufficiently wonder at this, since he has already settled accounts with Keij Aeria for the sum of 1500 rixdollars, and now again demands 2000, where there is no person in the world who can mention such a sum in his contract, but it seems that he now has no place to load the timber rafts, so much as circumstances allow to be hastened. The resident stands ready again to depart to Indramaju by Your Excellency's esteemed command, wherewith &c. was signed Isaac Ring, Elias Vredenhoff, and Lucas Munster, at the side of Sirebon in the fort of protection on the 2nd of June 1693. — Batavia To his Excellency the Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor, General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of India by inland voyage. From Sirebon on the 8th of June 1693: received the 12th of July 1693. Your Excellency's esteemed, Most Earnest, Great esteemed, Mighty, Wise, foresighted, generous Lords, Your Excellency's high commanding Lords. Our most humble submission to Your Excellency has been on the 2nd of this month, from Sirebon in the company of the yacht the Señor Nicolaes, with which vessel here at the roadstead on the 4th, I have again arrived safely, not doubting its safe passage to Batavia, which the Almighty grant. This my most entirely submissive [letter] shall now only serve as an accompaniment to the enclosed documents, namely a letter from the soldier Johannes Klein, on the 4th of this month from Imbanagara to the resident Ring, brought here yesterday evening. text_translated_detailed: The Demang Timbanganten has ordered the villages of Tsieparoe and the rice fields of Pamporan, Tcilinglampos, and Tietimkoerap, which he had taken from the Ingabeij Tsioetsioek, to be restored and has recommended that the same be allowed to possess them peacefully, since Van Indermaijo on the 8th of June 1693 clearly established that the Ingaben Tsioetsioek had the right to them, as not only the Kandoeroean Tchelassiouw, the Ingabeij Soetabaija, and the village of Saraija have testified here, but also moreover Wbira Diwangsa, Anga Soeta, and Maessouda Prana, all three being people of the Trommarogon Demang Timbanganten himself and who presently inhabit the aforementioned villages, according to the evidence sent to me by Joannes Kleijn, whereas against this Timbanganten could not produce a single witness from all his accompanying people for himself, and everything he brought forward, whether it was Tana Oeker, and it certainly belonged to him, notwithstanding his own people testified against him. He is an old fox who is not frightened by a small rumor, and with that he goes. To get it with, I first asked him whether he would follow my given evidence, then he said no. Then I asked him whether he approved of the same or not, that such would be equally much more esteemed, that it from Van Ondermaijoe on the 8th of June 1693 would nevertheless stand to be seized, and that neither he nor anyone of his should further trouble the villages of the Ingabeij Tsioetsioek, and if there should be anyone who would wrong him, then it should be made known to me, and then I would grant him equal right. Besides these village disputes, his people are strong 60 coppen, by violent hand of those of Praccan Moetjang no water could be obtained from there. I have told him in the good pleasure of Your Excellency's Worship that such conduct is well

From Sirbon on the 12th of July 1693, to the same person, and two others granted to go to Mataram and collect their debts, so we have deemed it best to first await Your Honored Excellency's esteemed order, so that we might conduct ourselves in all obedience according to that. His secret departure and return, as well as the fact that he had himself registered as an inhabitant of Samarang in order to go collect his debts along with the others in Mataram, gives us in Your Honored Excellency's favorable consideration, though we have some reservations whether there might not be something else hidden behind this, which we also did not wish to fail to give Your Excellency this humble notice of. With which, etc., it was signed Isaac Rhing, Elias vredenHoff [uncertain: vredenHoff], and Lucas Munster, standing beside it Sirbon in the fort the Protection on the 12th of July 1693. — Following the daily record kept by the Soldier Joannes Klein, on his journey to the forest Iatij rockie [uncertain: Iatij rockie], together with the encounters and findings observed on that journey, on the 5th of June departed from Imbanagara to Tangala and 9th of the same month. The soldier Jan Klein returned on the 27th of July at Sirbon, with the report that the timber forest so renowned by the Priangers, [which was said to contain] full-grown heavy trees, is but a poor common forest, and is situated four days' journey from Imbanagara, standing under the Tommogen Raxa Nagara, who has shown them good treatment. The Nietie Praja [Nietie Praja: a territorial or administrative division], taken from him by the Panambahan, the sultans have still not made an end of it, notwithstanding that it clearly appears that the Nietie Praja rightfully belongs [to him], as hundreds of people testify. The Panambahan, to date, has not been able to produce a single witness. We have repeatedly reminded the sultans Sopo and Annum of Your Honored Excellency's esteemed orders and commands, and urged and recommended them to follow them, but they pay no attention to them, and it appears to Your Honored Excellency's favorable consideration to be rather a jest with them than earnest. For when they, after long delay, have finally set a day to arbitrate, and we think it will come to pass, then they let it be known the day or evening before that they are unwell, and thus it goes back and forth. And when it finally happens that they are together, and no sickness is feigned, then the one will not hang the bell on the cat for the other, and the Panambahan then speaks the great word, without the sultans making the slightest move regarding the matter, which Your Honored Excellency has so earnestly commanded them to address or investigate. It is also to be believed that they [still] hold the Tommogen Nietie Praja. From Inder Majoe on the 5th of July 1693.

text_translated_detailed: and when it finally happens that they are together, and no one feigns illness, then neither one will hang the bell on the cat for the other, and the Panambahan then takes the lead in the matter, without the sultans making the slightest movement regarding the affair, which has been so earnestly recommended to them by Your Honour, to touch upon or investigate it. It is also my belief that they, the Tonmogen Nietie praija of Indermajoe on the 5th of July 1693, will still do what is right, although they know well enough that the Panambahan has wronged them. Moreover, the Sultans would then, in Your Honour's favourable consideration, pronounce their own judgment, for the Pangeran of Calaga has, in the year before last, had half his land and people taken from him, and sold to another who was the Pangeran's servant, for 500 rixdollars [modern equivalent: a substantial sum]; and besides this Pangeran, there are still 7 or 8 free chiefs, among whom there is also a Pangeran Sueria Mangala, who would all gladly submit themselves to the Company's obedience, if only the way were first opened by the Tommogon Wierat macka. This one has made his complaint to me about how the Panambahan has had his wife, whom he has now kept away from him for a considerable time, finally locked up in prison, and has requested my assistance in this matter. Whereupon I had the Sultans approached, as they were gathered together, that they would be pleased to summon the aforementioned woman and restore her to her husband, which the Sultans ordered the Tanabahan to do, who answered them that he would not do such a thing. Such and similar is their conduct, which is too much to trouble Your Honour with any longer. With this I remain and was signed Isaac Ring, at the side of Indermajoe in the Company's warehouse on the 5th of July 1643, and below it received by the fluyt Eglenburg on the 5th of August 1693.

text_translated_detailed: From Sirbon on the 28th of September 1693. Batavia To His Honourable Excellency Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honourable Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands India by express hired fishing vessel, in the hands of the Javanese dourie, Most Honourable, esteemed, manly, aforementioned, very generous Gentlemen, received on the 1st of October 1693. Well Honourable, commanding Gentlemen, the Chaloupe [small sailing vessel] the Hengelaer and the patchall [patrol vessel] the Koningsvis, which Your Honour has been pleased to send as escort for the now readied four wood rafts, hereward, and for which we remain very humbly grateful to Your Honour, have arrived here at the roadstead the day before yesterday in good order, after having unloaded the goods brought with them for the use of the wood rafts at Indermaijoe, whereby we have well received Your Honour's esteemed letter of the 18th of the current month, from which we see that the fluytes [merchant ships] Eglenburg and Brondosee are to come to us within a few days, the first mentioned since it has a cargo permit with a load of beams and heavy timber work, and the other to fetch the remainder of the whole legger tiles, upon their appearance we shall not fail from Sirbon on the 28th of September 1693.— to provide the same with their cargo as speedily as possible, and if it should happen that the fluyte Brondosee cannot obtain its full cargo at Indermaijoe, the same in conformity with Your Honour's much esteemed order and commands at Ponmanaskan and Tsiassen shall be loaded, to fill its remaining hold with legger tiles and other light timber work, for which reason we have sent ahead the Malay Abdul Gaine with the patchall the Koningsvis and our letter to the chiefs there in that direction, to recommend to them the timber work already ordered for them, to be brought ready down together, as the bookkeeper Christiaen Krijger has promised them, since Your Honour has been pleased to send a vessel for their transport,

text_translated_detailed: From Sirbon on the 23rd of October 1693, with which &c. was signed: Elias Vredenhoff and Lucas Munster, beside which stood Sirbon in fort the protection on the 23rd of October 1693. Batavia. To His High Excellency the Lord W. van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Councils of the Netherlands India, His High Excellency, greatly esteemed. The ship the King of Bantam received on the 3rd of September 1693, as aforesaid, generous Lords. Since the submissive letter dated the 23rd of this month from Sirbon through the Chinese Thoko, the assistant minister has thereupon come here again over the land route, in order to follow Your Excellency's much esteemed order, the ship the King of Bantam, after receiving a cargo of heavy timber work, to send to Your High Excellency, as the same now goes to Your High Excellency with a quantity of 132 pieces of sorted beams 67 [units], planks for gun carriages 5500 [units], whole barrel staves, which after the dispatch from Eglenburg came again from the timber forests, and have been loaded for complete stowage in the aforementioned vessel. From Indermajo on the 30th of October 1693. The Sergeant Jan Jacobsz van Merwe from Ghent, together with the military personnel, permitted by His High Excellency's high esteem to come to Batavia, are now proceeding in conformity with the latest letter from Sirbon, as now through this vessel for His High Excellency, as is shown in the accompanying name roll in Your Excellency's esteemed very humble and complete submission. The Ingabeij Wiera Loddra stands ready within a few days, with his accompanying vessels and rice cargo of more than 100 coyang [uncertain: unit of measurement], to undertake the journey through Batavia for Your Excellency's esteemed direction. This thus far written, received over the land route from Sirbon, a letter from the Commanding Sergeant Elias Vredenhoff, serving as principal notice, how that after the departure of the assistant from there, from the upper lands a fine shipment of cardamom had been brought, but would with the receipt thereof wait so long as the aforementioned Munster appeared there again, when we shall not fail to give Your Excellency humble notice thereof, in hope that the shipment shall yet increase and thus the requested matter for His High Excellency for the fatherland we shall be able to provide, to which as much as possible, all efforts shall be employed to be able to give Your Excellency complete satisfaction. text_translated_detailed: From Indermajoe on the 30th of October 1693, with a ship of 100 coyang [uncertain: possibly a type of vessel or cargo measure], the journey to be undertaken to Batavia under Your Honour's esteemed direction. text_translated_detailed: I do not wonder that they say this, since Intij Pradja and Ebirad Macka, six lanega [uncertain: possibly a measure or administrative division] as they remain in the Company's fortress under the authority of the Resident, shall yet burden me all the more, therefore I beseech most humbly Your Honour, that this lingering matter may come to a speedy end, for I am shamed through the loss of my former status, the more so because the Honourable Company has made me great, and drawn me into the number of the three princes brothers, and now such an Intij Pradja and Eiradmoncka, who are my own subjects, with the mockery, this is hard to bear, and they also say that they are regents who have 500 heads under their authority, whereas on the contrary all the Sirbonders well know that it is an hereditary right of my forefathers and my own people, and if 500 can be taken from it, then my good name as one of the three princes brothers shall be damaged and gone, for I can complain to no one else but the Company, after having made Contract with me I must regulate myself, and therefore I request once more from Your Honour that From Sirebon on October 1693, Netij Pradja and Wierad Macka be handed over to me, and concerning this matter with my envoys, as they depart for home, a small letter may be written to Sirebon, and that from the name of the Honourable Company finally, and I have nothing else to present to the Mister Major but half a last [modern equivalent: approximately 1,500 kg] of rice and two beasts of burden, with the request that the little may be excused, being but the flower without scent. text_translated_detailed: From Sirbon, the 13th of November 1693. Batavia. To His High Excellency, the Lord Mr. Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Lords, Councillors of the Netherlands Indies, by the Chinese voyage. Your High Excellency, most esteemed, most worthy, most prudent, most generous and most noble governing Lords. After the dispatch of the yacht the King of Bantam with a cargo of timber from Soemermaijoe to your well-esteemed High Excellency, the Assistant Munster arrived here safely on the first of this month by the overland route from there, and subsequently in the Company's fortress on various days from diverse Priangan chiefs, we received a quantity of 31½ pounds of Cardamom, as well as above the recently noted 50 pounds of pepper, delivered by the authorized agents of the Captain of the Chinese, Ki'aria Marta Nata, amounting to more than 135 pounds, so that now of this commodity here we have a quantity of more than 475 pounds in stock, with which it appears this season will proceed further. On the 22nd of this month, we received a Javanese letter from Prackan Moetjang, wherein complaint was made of how there four Chinese had been detained for some time in the pursuit of their trade, and thereby the Javanese had been robbed of their goods, which aforementioned Chinese claimed back from the chiefs of that village, requesting our assistance therein, which we have deemed fit to answer in accordance with Your High Excellency's great esteem, that when the aforementioned Chinese from Sirbon should come to appear here, we would ascertain the truth of that matter, as they then arrived on the 5th of this month with the names Kinko, Inko, Ionko, and Lauko, all inhabitants here, who made their complaint in the manner aforesaid, namely that they had been in that place as well as in Samadang and Calago, and had remained 2 months and 10 days in those

text_translated_detailed: it has not been unwelcome to us, the approval taken by your Excellency after the unloading of the flutes Bronste and Eglenburg, as well as the yacht the King of Bantam, just as we likewise hope to understand from this, which we according to your High Excellency's much esteemed order with the pepper here in stock, together with the Cardamom and some few cloves, as much as has been possible, have sent back at the earliest, just as now— they have been loaded, and to your Excellency passes with a quantity of 308½ pounds or 38,850 catties [modern equivalent: traditional Asian weight unit] of black pepper, 30½ pounds or 3,050 catties of Javanese Cardamom, 1,000 pieces of whole barrel cloves, and 6 pots with wet Indigo, costing with the other according to the accompanying invoice and the expenses incurred in the shipping thereof a sum of ƒ6,447.15. for which we shall not fail, under the favorable consideration of your High Excellency, to charge the general Office properly, and there remains now here still a quantity with the returned pepper of about 120 pounds in stock, which has been a sorrow to us because of the smallness of the hold of the aforementioned small vessel, in which it could not have been shipped. And since with the now brought cash we are again provided in such a way as to be able to satisfy the suppliers now owing to the Esteemed Company, we shall not fail to follow your High Excellency's much esteemed order, and whereby suitably then again the same shall be brought to an even footing, just as we shall also endeavor to follow this, so that at each delivery everyone receives what is theirs, and further await your Excellency's further commands, just as also the remaining number above the ru. text_translated_detailed: Here within the Company's fortress were brought three Javanese by the names of Lambon, Singa Goena, and Ebala, residing in the village of Gessik belonging under the Pang. Panamboehom, who were charged with the murder of a certain Chinese named 'Tsouko, an inhabitant here. However, after examining them, we found that the perpetrator of this deed had taken flight into the territory of the aforementioned Panembahan, and they had served to assist in bringing the murdered Chinese into the forest and burying him. Therefore, the aforementioned three persons, under the favorable approval of Your Excellency, were taken into custody for the time being, and we demanded the Pangeran Panambahan of the north by the name of Iaja Laxana to hand them over, so that they could then be delivered together into the hands of the Sultans Soppo and Annom, and each according to their merit for the deed committed receive their deserved punishment at Cirebon on the 18th of December 1643. However, the Panambahan, when asked about the aforementioned murderer, claimed to know nothing of him from anywhere and said he did not have such a Javanese in his territory. Yet there was sufficient evidence of this, and moreover it is not unusual for him to harbor such guests. We therefore deemed it best to place the aforementioned three persons in the hands of the aforementioned Sultans and to hand over the matter to them, with the recommendation to endeavor to get the perpetrator into their hands, which we then delivered to them. text_translated_detailed: Received by the free burgher Leendert Veerman on the 31st of January 1694. From Cirebon on the 18th of December 1693. And Sultan Annam, since the death of his first wife Ratoe Paninga in the recently passed month of November, has entirely, according to his own account, settled into a quiet and peaceful life, wishing to involve himself in nothing, and has given his first son Pangeran Ratoe the direction to administer his affairs, for which the latter is sufficiently capable to play his role properly. Yet this shall not cause us to neglect to have the necessary care for him as well as for the rest, and to exercise the required foresight in one and another matter. With which, etc., it was signed Elias Vredenhof and Lucas Munster in the margin at Cirebon in the fort of protection on the 18th of December 1693. Batavia. To His Excellency, the Mister W. W. van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen, Councillors of India. Most Esteemed Gentlemen, greatly honored, Most Earnest, Mighty, Wise, Foresighted, Generous Gentlemen, Most Esteemed Commanding Gentlemen. By the Jagje de Fortuin, our last most humble letter has been received together with its cargo of 363 pounds of pepper and 500 pounds of whole logs, to Your Excellency's great advantage. From Cirebon on the 4th of January 1694, it departed; which we hope will have reached Your Excellency by now, and as after the completion of that small vessel, as the aforementioned Your Excellency had submitted in the postscript at that time in all humility, how within one or two days yet a quantity of about 70 pounds of pepper was to come, which we then, under the favorable approval and wise judgment, deemed best to hold for the time being, while the free burgher Leendert Veerman, resident of Batavia, with his new Chaloupe named the Hope, was lying here at the roadstead, and had no cargo of significance to transport with it.

text_translated_detailed: In the aforementioned postscript to Your Honour, we have humbly reported that within one or two days a further quantity of approximately 70 piculs [modern equivalent: ~4,200 kg] of pepper was expected to arrive, which we would then accept under your favourable and wise judgment, at such time as the free burgher Leendert Veerman, resident of Batavia, was lying here at the roadstead with his new Chaloupe [small sailing vessel] named the Hope, and having no cargo of significance to transport with it, we presented it to him, and gladly whatever served the Company's interests, insofar as it was within our power, we wished to promote. In this matter, Your Honour's great esteem permitted us to load not only the aforementioned pepper, but also a quantity of 101½ piculs [modern equivalent: ~6,090 kg] net that we obtained together from Sultan Anon as well as some Priangan [region in West Java] chiefs, which we hope will not be unwelcome to you, and which together was shipped in the said Chaloupe, amounting with some minor expenses incurred in the loading, according to the accompanying bill of lading and invoice, which Your Honour will see in all humility, to a sum of ƒ2,002.6.12, for which we shall not fail to properly debit the General Office in your favourable acceptance. By postscript of the aforementioned letter from Sirbon [Seribu Islands] on 21 January 1694, we have also noted how the aforementioned free burgher requested of us that, since his anchor equipment was not yet well provided for, in order to secure his voyage before the ordering of the western monsoon to Batavia, he might be helped with an anchor and rope, and use them on loan until his arrival in Batavia. Therefore, in your favourable acceptance, we could not refuse him this, and we deemed this help necessary against the Company's service, as he was transporting the aforementioned quantity of pepper without us requesting anything for it. We have arranged this under proper handwriting, as Your Honour will see adjoined hereto in all humility.

text_translated_detailed: From Tanjoupoura in the year 1692. Brief summary of the content of the Javanese petition, from Tambak baija to Their High Excellencies, the Governor General, and the Esteemed lords councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Your Excellency's humble servant respectfully submits that during the time of the Esteemed Governor General Rijkloff van Goens, of blessed memory, and since then until now, all that which has been assigned to him regarding the service of the East India Company by the Tommogon, he, as the eldest of the ten Ombols, or chief men, under the said Tommogon, has diligently fulfilled and performed in all respects. Furthermore, I must say that I have been unable to obtain any other horses here, with which, after most humble greetings, this letter shall conclude in the present, as my intentions are stated in the aforementioned letter. Batavia. To His Excellency, the Esteemed Lord Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. From Tanjoupoura on the last of March 1693. — Esteemed, strict, honourable gentlemen, aforementioned, generous Lords, Esteemed, high commanding Lords. After my most humble submission of the 9th of February had been sent to Your Honour and Excellency, on the 12th and thereafter on the sacred days of Marta Mangala, the chiefs belonging under Keij Aria Wira Saba came to report to me that on the night that had just passed, at the small village of Sumanka, there had been thieves who, by means of mining, had managed to enter the house of the Javanese Wangsa Karta, and there took away: one copper Javanese rice pot, a cup with two cloths, one fish trap net, one small copper basin, and one ballion or axe. But the aforementioned Javanese Wangsa Karta, meanwhile becoming alarmed and making a loud noise about it, everything came into alarm, and they went together (the thieves meanwhile choosing the Hasepar path) to search for those unwelcome guests, whom they pursued into the forest, near the small village of Babaccan Diatie, approximately one hour's journey from the first aforementioned place from Tansonpoura on the last of March 1693, but when those rogues found themselves pursued, they set off running, but the Javanese Marta Bangsa, catching up with them, struck down with a spear,

Martin had been sent, which I respectfully trust, not doubting that Your Honors will receive complete knowledge thereof, here have arrived some envoys from the Demang Timbamanting in Bandong, also bringing some poor unsuitable horses, except two which are reasonably good, for which they claim 35 Spanish reals Spanish silver coins, which have come here by their own people under the supervision of the native soldier Jan Pietersz. from Batavia, since according to the esteemed ordinance of the esteemed Major he has been permitted to come to Batavia once to have himself united in the married state, and since at that very time another horse of the Tommogen Tanoebaija, his Sourouans, and another of Carte Iaja at Nambo has come to be sold, I have deemed it best, with Your Honors' permission, to let these also pass through, if they might please Your Honors, with the Tommogon Tanoebaija's people claiming 25 reals and Carta Iaja but 12 reals for their horse, which they are however leaving to Your Honors' decision, and whatever Your Honors are pleased to give them, the Tommogen Tanoebaija will remain grateful. From Tanjoupoura on the 19th of May 1693.

text_translated_detailed: From Tanjoupoura on the 27th of August 1693. I inquired about the appearance of the aforementioned group of logs, asking whose they were and what logs they were, and why they had not been sent off together with the others. To this he replied that it was the Company's and Souta Iouda's fault that they still lay there, and at the same time asking Souta Souda why this had come about. He gave no other answer to this than that it had happened through a mistake, without showing any concern about it, even though he noticed that Keij Maes was displeased about it. Whereupon the Ombol Anga Patra was ordered by Keij Maes to send off the remaining logs, which indeed happened accordingly. Meanwhile I also learned from various sources that Souta Iouda observed the orders of Keij Maes very little, considering that he was the greatest and oldest Ombol [headman]; and for this reason he was also feared and respected by the other Ombols. Keij Maes was particularly praised and beloved by the common people and the Ombols on account of his mild and reasonable manner of dealing, and also because when they received payment for the sold timber, they were also treated well and gently according to the Javanese method. He believed that as soon as the remainder of what was requested had been cut by the Ingabeij, by the coming full moon according to his estimate, it would be brought to Batavia, for which purpose I gave him the necessary speed in the name of Your Honored Excellency, and at the same time requested that the remaining logs already lying ready be sent off. With this, along with a polite greeting from me to Carta Jouda, he went upstream. text_translated_detailed: September 7, 1693. From Tanjoupoura. Translation of a Javanese letter by Demang Timbananting to Bandong, sent to the Venerable Sas at Canjonpoura and from there received at Batavia on [date] 1693. This letter comes from me, Daman Timbananting to Bandong, to my brother the Vendrij [ensign] Anthonij Sas at Tanjonpoura, to whom I shall make known, along with my greetings, what sort of settlements have been under my authority since ancient times, except for the three rice fields of Wiera Diwangsa, Anga Souta, and Iouda Drana, over which settlements there has never been any dispute or disagreement. As for the names of the settlements: Sada Touwang Kandatouan, where a Maradja [chief] stands in charge, houses: 13. Vundel Hawel, D.O. Souta Saraija: 4. Sarantaka: 10. Tsiwalo: 4. C. Sadij Tschinmet: 3. Thitajum: 5. Transported houses: 98. Higarok. Nibij Joek. From Tanjonpoura under date September 7, 1693. Transport outside.

text_translated_detailed: Received in September, October from Tanjungpoura [Tanjung Pura] dated September 7, 1691, by the envoys of the Tommogon Tanubaija. The fugitive Javanese are staying in the surroundings of Tsilingsing, where they have erected nothing but huts or shelters. The bearer of this letter is my brother Kinthol Darpa Goena. Everything I have to say is written herein. Batavia. To the Honored Gentlemen Joan van Hoorn, Director General, and Isaac de Martin, Councilor of the Order of India. Honored, strict, esteemed, wise, foresighted, and most generous Gentlemen. Honored commanding Gentlemen, these my most humble and obedient services are solely at the request of the Tommogon Panata Iouda, who humbly requests that while the commanders of Soeta Iouda cannot be made to change their opinion (just as I have also approached them with all kindness and, moreover, have previously laid out the consequences that would result from this), in order to remain under Soeta Ioeda, they might obtain another chief, whomever it might please your Honored Excellencies to appoint. From Tanjungpoura, the 27th of September 1693. So that those provisions might not be lost, it is arranged that he shall take care that they will gradually return again to Soera Ioeda, since they first wish to receive restitution from those goods that Soeta Ioeda has brought in above what he produced at his accounting, and since we with his and he with our temperament can always get along well, I would be willing to accommodate him in this, provided that it came to agreement with your Honored Excellencies' good intention and no further consequences arose. Therefore, your Honored Excellencies' wise judgment, with all due diligence in this matter, shall await how I am to conduct myself with those peoples regarding Soeta Ioeda. With the new moon, the palisade wood, which is now being felled, will be ready, and if it pleases your Excellencies, they would gladly deliver a greater quantity than has been recommended to them to collect. Furthermore, having nothing more to write than the health of these post holders and the condition of the Cradang quarters, I shall conclude under your Excellencies' good pleasure, and remain under your Honored Excellencies' protection, etc. And was signed A. Glas. In the margin stood: Tanjungpoura in the field fortification, the 27th of September 1693.

text_translated_detailed: Received the 28th of October 1693, per the Anbol Sourentacka. From Tanjungpoura, the 18th of October 1693. Batavia. To the Honored Gentlemen Joan van Hoorn, Director General, and Isaac S. Martin, Councilor, Council of all the East India Company. Honored, strict, esteemed, wise, foresighted, and most generous Gentlemen. Honored commanding Gentlemen, these my most humble and obedient services are solely in accompaniment of the Ombol Soerantacka, who today is being sent off by the Tommogen with 47 boats of timber wood for the East India Company, according to the attached provided list, to which we respectfully defer. The returning ones coming next month, according to their account, will likewise be ready. But since some ombols have already shipped quite poor quality timber, for which reason at the distribution of money they will receive as much as those who delivered good timber, the Tommog. very earnestly requests that your Honored Excellencies be pleased to order that each ombol's timber wood be valued separately, so that when they are deceived in their expectation, at another time they will be better inclined to deliver according to their duty. The Loeras or overseers of Soeto Ioeda have given me on the 4th of this month a detailed account of what Soeta Ioeda should have deducted from his 13-year account of theirs. From Tanjungpoura, the 18th of October 1693. Herewith your Honored Excellencies receive the consumption account of the month of September, together with the name roll of the post holders, whose health is reasonably good, except for one Ropiaense soldier Jacob Jacuno, who is somewhat impotent, as well as a letter from the Tommogon Panata Zoudo, the Ombol Tambakbaja, and Ebiera Bega, which two latter very reverently request, just as they also do on their behalf, that the Javanese in chains there, Hoeta Craoan and Zimeija, might be released from the same and sent back. For the present, I have nothing more to write than that the Cravang chiefs are visibly in agreement with one another in all things, it being to be wished that those under the command of Hoeta Iuda would be willing to sort themselves under him as their former chiefs. From Tanjung Poura, the 18th of October 1693. Martin raad ordinaris en Maijoor van Jndia, tot batavia, ontfangen 30. October 1693: Na vele groete, zend ik tommog: panata souda, als een dienaer van d' EComp. en, tot Carta Iassa, dit

text_original: Van Tanjonpoura Anno 1693. Translaet van een Javaens briefje, door den Javaen astra Iouda, tot batavia den Laesten October 1643. den Javaen genaemt asra souda, maeke bij dit geschrift bekent, aen haer Ho: Ed: agtb: tot batavia, hoe dat hij voor desen nog eens heeft geklaegt, over het ongelijk dat hem was aengedaen, door den Tommogon soukapoura, die hem zijn gesag en volk hadde afgenomen, waer op uEd: dan den Jawaense Luijtenam praija wangsa, in die tijd na boven hebben gesonden, om na de waerheijt van dese zaek te vernemen; gelijk gemelte Luijtenant mijn aenbrengen dan ook regt matig bevonden, en mij, mijn volk en gesag, weder gegeven heeft, over een en deselve zaek, kom ik uEd: nu weder moeijlijk vallen, wam den hommogon wiera daka, hooft regent tot soekapawa,— heeft mij van mijn voorouders erffregt, bestaende in een getal van 147. huijs gesinnen berooft, enhoud, dan volk onder zijn gesag, hier op sal ik uEd: ordre afwagten eijnde. Batavia Aan de Ed: Heren Joan van Hoorn directeur generaal, en Isaac ds„r martin Raad ordinaris van Gants India Van Tanjonpoura Anno 1693. text_translated_detailed: From Tanjon Poura, Anno 1693. Translation of a Javanese letter, by the Javanese Astra Iouda, to Batavia on the last of October 1643. The Javanese named Asra Souda makes known by this writing to Your Honors' Esteemed Lordships in Batavia, how that he has previously once more complained about the injustice that was done to him by the Tommogon Soukapoura, who had taken from him his authority and people, whereupon Your Honors then sent the Javanese Lieutenant Praija Wangsa at that time upriver to ascertain the truth of this matter; just as the aforementioned Lieutenant found my complaint to be entirely justified and has returned to me my people and authority, over this same matter I now come to trouble Your Honors again, for the Hommogon Wiera Daka, chief regent of Soekapawa, has robbed me of my ancestral hereditary right, consisting of a number of 147 household families, and holds this people under his authority, whereupon I shall await Your Honors' order herein. Batavia. To the Esteemed Gentlemen Joan van Hoorn, Director General, and Isaac [uncertain: ds„r] Martin, Ordinary Councilor of East India. From Tanjon Poura, Anno 1693. text_translated_detailed: From Tanjon Poura, Anno 1693. Translation of a Javanese letter, by the Javanese Astra Iouda, to Batavia on the last of October 1643. The Javanese named Asra Souda makes known by this writing to Your Honors' Esteemed Lordships in Batavia, how that he has previously once more complained about the injustice that was done to him by the Tommogon Soukapoura, who had taken from him his authority and people, whereupon Your Honors then sent the Javanese Lieutenant Praija Wangsa at that time upriver to ascertain the truth of this matter; just as the aforementioned Lieutenant found my complaint to be entirely justified and has returned to me my people and authority, over this same matter I now come to trouble Your Honors again, for the Hommogon Wiera Daka, chief regent of Soekapawa, has robbed me of my ancestral hereditary right, consisting of a number of 147 household families, and holds this people under his authority, whereupon I shall await Your Honors' order herein. Batavia. To the Esteemed Gentlemen Joan van Hoorn, Director General, and Isaac [uncertain: ds„r] Martin, Ordinary Councilor of East India, on the 17th of November 1693. From Tanjon Houra, the 16th of November 1693. Esteemed, Your Honors, valiant [uncertain: ontfangen e. r een oera], wise, aforementioned, and generous [uncertain: steven d:] Your Honors commanding stars. After my most humble submission, accompanied by the Ombol Soerantacka on the 18th of the past month of October had departed with a shipment of ambaro wood for Your Honors' Commander, so on the 7th of this month from the Ombol Sacra Dita, Kiaij Neija Praija, belonging under Keij Aria Wiera Saba, were further sent off on 5 rafts of 650 bamboos [modern equivalent: bamboo poles] and 225 ambaro wood, and on the 13th thereof, again from Sacra Dita 107 [uncertain: d. o] Caijate, likewise from Marta Mangala 150 ambaro wood and that on 5 rafts of 660 bamboos, and the remaining from the Tommogon

text_translated_detailed: October had departed with a shipment of ambaro wood for Your Honors' Commander, so on the 7th of this month from the Ombol Sacra Dita, Kiaij Neija Praija, belonging under Keij Aria Wiera Saba, were further sent off on 5 rafts of 650 bamboos [modern equivalent: bamboo poles] and 225 ambaro wood, and on the 13th thereof, again from Sacra Dita 107 [uncertain: d. o] Caijate, likewise from Marta Mangala 150 ambaro wood and that on 5 rafts of 660 bamboos, and the remaining from the Tommogon Panoeta Touda and Kiaij Wiera Saba, according to their statement, are to follow every day, for which they are pressed daily as much as is possible. The Javanese Wiera Wangsa from Siassem with his household has come here quietly, to settle himself here, having at the request of Angabeij Carta Joeda, to his emissary the Loera Surga Watsiana, who gave us direction where he was staying, according to Contract immediately restored, who again on the 3rd of this month has departed therewith with promises that some from here, from those insights also came there, they would be assured each time in like manner to return here. On the 14th of this month, a man Timbenanting in Bandang, his emissary named Ianga Marta, with some horses, cattle, and further small items of gifts, departed from here by land road to Costij [Kosti] without having wished to reveal to us anything more of what his business is. The Chinese Onjnko, inhabitant of Batavia, has on the 9th of this month made an agreement with the Crawangsa [Krauwangsah] Chiefs, provided that it pleases Your Honors to allow this, whereby he promises all the firewood that they can cut, provided that they must deliver it to Costij outside the Rotterdam gate, as follows: 100 pieces [modern equivalent: stx: = stukken/pieces] of 4 feet long and 3 to 4 spans [modern equivalent: span = approximately 9 inches or 23 cm] thick for 2¼ rixdollars [modern equivalent: rd:s = rixdollars] per 100. From Tanjoupoura, the 16th of November 1690, was given to his mate Pieter Hendricksz., who faithfully cared for him in his illness, but his full weapons being stored in the weapons chamber, was properly debited therefor. Coppen, wel is bestelt, ook heb ik ten eersten ordre gegeven en belast, dat men aen zoeta Joeda zijn volk soude ter hand stellen, doende alles wat in mijn vermogen is geweest, ook heb ik twaelf babackels, die onwillig waren, bij den vendrig Las gebragt, daerse int blok zijn gesloten, en tgemene volk (makende een Compagnie) heb ik moeten dwingen, om weder bij soeta Toeda tegaen, stellende zig gesamentlijk tegens d' ordre van d' EComp. e, als zijnde niet genegen onder souta Iouda te sorteren: nu isfer een goet getal van dat volk weg gelopen, agterlatende hunne vrouwen en kinderen, maer de babakkels (of Corporaels) blyven nog in't blok zitten, tot nader ordre, van uEd: Ho agtb:, en het gemene volk, wil niet langer van zoeta Joeda gecommandeert werden, om de weg gelopene Javanen t' agterhalen, heb ik eenig volk uijtgesonden: wat ik hebbe teseggen staet in dit briefje geschreven. eijnde. text_translated_detailed: From Tanjonpoura dated the 27th of December 1693. Translation of a Javanese letter, by the Tommogon Panata Jouda to Cirebon, sent to Your Honour to Batavia, received in December 1693. After many greetings, the Tommogon Panata Souda sends, as a servant of the Company in Cirebon, this letter to the Honourable Sir and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Honourable gentlemen councillors of India, to Batavia. Furthermore, it should be made known to Your Honour that Your Honour's letter regarding the people of Soeta Jouda, consisting of 87 heads, has been duly received. I have also given orders at the earliest opportunity and instructed that the people of Soeta Jouda be handed over to him, doing everything within my power. I have also brought twelve babackels [corporals] who were unwilling to the ensign Las, where they have been locked in the stocks, and the common people (forming a company) I have had to compel to return to Soeta Jouda, as they collectively set themselves against the order of the Company, being unwilling to serve under Souta Jouda. Now a good number of those people have run away, leaving behind their wives and children, but the babackels (or corporals) remain still in the stocks, pending further orders from Your Honour. And the common people will no longer be commanded by Soeta Jouda. To pursue the Javanese who have run away, I have sent out some people. What I have to say is written in this letter. Ending. From Tanjoupoura dated the 27th of December 1683. Those who are stuck in the palisade request pardon, was signed Tommogon Panata Jonda, Singamangala, Tambakbaija, Wira Baija, Astra Jouda, Naija Raga, and Pitra Souta. Translation of a Javanese letter written by the Ombol Tamback Baija to Cirebon, to Your Honour to Batavia, received in December.

Received per Waddingsveen, Noble Honorable Gentlemen, on the 14th February 1693. — From the Cape of Good Hope on the 26th November 1692. — Noble Honorable Gentlemen. — On the 30th of September we last had the honor to write to Your Most Esteemed Honors with the ship Sir Jan's Land. Meanwhile, on the 20th of October, the ships Crap, Nieuwland, and Tambour took harbor, and the following day Ytershem with the galiot the Rruijm [uncertain: possibly a ship name]. These five ships sailed together on the 25th of May from Texel and around the north of Scotland. They refreshed themselves together from the 9th of July to the 16th following at St. Jago, where they learned from the Portuguese that approximately five months before they had been there — four French ships, which had claimed to be heading to the East Indies, so that we can only conclude that they are the same ships of which we gave Your Most Esteemed Honors notice in our aforementioned letter of the 30th of September. The aforesaid ships lost 176 men on the voyage through sickness.
