Noble, Earnest, valiant, prudent, and most generous Lord, and Esteemed Lords. By the fluyt ship the Dove, received at Batavia on the 21st of February 1693. — Esteemed and Most Honorable Lords. Just as it pleased the Esteemed Lord Simon van der Stel — Governor at the Cape of Good Hope — from Mauritius on the 1st of December, Year 1692, to appoint us to replace the former chief of the island of Mauritius, the Esteemed Isaacq Johannes Lamatius, Abraham Steen, and Jacob Ovaar in their year of service, we were dismissed on the 26th of the previous month of August, together with the fluyt the Dove from the aforementioned Cape, and that same evening we set sail. And God be praised, on the 22nd of the month of October (without having experienced any notable storms or any deaths on the journey) we came to anchor in the South-East harbor of this island. The aforementioned Esteemed Lord Governor van der Stel was pleased to give us knowledge of Your Esteemed Highness's secret missive dated the 25th of March 1691. And thereby ordered us to follow the tenor of the same exactly, just as we now come to report to Your Esteemed Highness with humble respect concerning what has transpired. text_translated_detailed: From Mauritius dated the 1st of August, Anno 1692, Cape of Good Hope. To the Honorable Lord Simon van der Stel, Governor and Esteemed Council. Honorable, Earnest, Magnanimous and Generous Lord and Esteemed Friends. On the 26th of the month of August of this year in the forenoon we departed with the small fluyt ship the Dove (as Your Esteemed Highness is aware) from Table Bay. On the 28th with the evening tide we lost sight of the land of the Cape. Subsequently we sailed with a south-southwest and south course until the 3rd of September at a southern latitude of 40 degrees 17 minutes, when we encountered the west trade wind. With the same we sailed east until the 2nd of the month of August, when we had a latitude of 30 degrees 16 minutes and an estimated longitude of approximately 90 degrees. Then we set our course northward and continued the same until the 7th of that month, when we had the latitude of Mauritius. From Mauritius dated the 1st of December, Anno 1692, we approached from the west. On the 18th thereof we sighted the island Diego Rodrigues, and on the 21st following, Mauritius, where on the 21st thereof (God be praised) with the aforementioned ship we arrived safely in the southeast harbor for anchorage without experiencing any remarkable storms or any deaths on the voyage. For a suitable person we found none, except for a certain Pieter Gerritsz van Stockholm with the boat of the remaining English ship Spreeuws burrij who landed here, who for now 1½ to 2 years has been employed in the service of the Esteemed Company in the forests without earning any wages. From this consideration we have therefore (under Your Esteemed Highness's approval) appointed the same as baas houtkapper [master woodcutter] at ƒ14 per month, as he is very knowledgeable in forestry, moreover a good woodcutter and sawyer, and therefore very useful to the Company, without whom we would have been somewhat at a loss. We shall present to Your Esteemed Highness, as briefly and clearly as we are able, and insofar as the shortness of our time here permits, the condition of the Company's operations and effects here. And first we begin with the lodge or rather Fort Fredrik Hendrik, of which the rear side is enclosed with a stone warehouse and dwelling house (in which there are 4 rooms, but two without cellars and unfinished), just as also a portion of the left side of this square is provided with a stone guardhouse. And although the other side is nearly completed, not one door of the warehouse is large enough to bring in a barrel, and nearly all the windows and door frames of this stone construction are destroyed by the worm (which reigns greatly here) and by the air due to lack of tar, so that they necessarily must be renewed. From Mauritius dated the 1st of December, Anno 1693, when the doors will be made larger and more suitable. The right side is nothing but a structure of boards, from which also the roof of the stone house is made, which is particularly dangerous on account of fire, and for which (this remaining thus) one is in no way secure. And should a fire break out, it is nearly impossible to save even one's own life. The side facing the sea is enclosed with a stone wall of a man's height high, which due to the poor foundation upon which it is built is nearly falling apart, and necessarily, if anything good is to be made of it, must be torn down and rebuilt. Outside of this is a half-moon shape enclosed with palisades, most of which are lying about and decaying. And between these lie 11 pieces of 3 and 4 pounder iron cannons, some of which have gun carriages and some without, but most of them are unusable. There still remain here from Mauritius dated the 1st of December, Anno 1692, two pieces of 2 pounder metal cannons, the gun carriages of which are also old and worm-eaten. On the left side, where the hill upon which this building rests rises up in height, stand some trees enclosed with palisades, where also some earth fruits grow. For a suitable person we found none, except for a certain Pieter Gerritsz van Stockholm with the boat of the remaining English ship Spreeuws burrij who landed here, who for now 1½ to 2 years has been employed in the service of the Esteemed Company in the forests without earning any wages. From this consideration we have therefore (under Your Esteemed Highness's approval) appointed the same as baas houtkapper master woodcutter at ƒ14 per month, as he is very knowledgeable in forestry, moreover a good woodcutter and sawyer, and therefore very useful to the Company, without whom we would have been somewhat at a loss. We shall present to Your Esteemed Highness, as briefly and clearly as we are able, and insofar as the shortness of our time here permits, the condition of the Company's operations and effects here. And first we begin with the lodge or rather Fort Fredrik Hendrik, of which the rear side is enclosed with a stone warehouse and dwelling house (in which there are 4 rooms, but two without cellars and unfinished), just as also a portion of the left side of this square is provided with a stone guardhouse. And although the other side is nearly completed, not one door of the warehouse is large enough to bring in a barrel, and nearly all the windows and door frames of this stone construction are destroyed by the worm (which reigns greatly here) and by the air due to lack of tar, so that they necessarily must be renewed. From Mauritius dated the 1st of December, Anno 1693, when the doors will be made larger and more suitable. The right side is nothing but a structure of boards, from which also the roof of the stone house is made, which is particularly dangerous on account of fire, and for which (this remaining thus) one is in no way secure. And should a fire break out, it is nearly impossible to save even one's own life. The side facing the sea is enclosed with a stone wall of a man's height high, which due to the poor foundation upon which it is built is nearly falling apart, and necessarily, if anything good is to be made of it, must be torn down and rebuilt. Outside of this is a half-moon shape enclosed with palisades, most of which are lying about and decaying. And between these lie 11 pieces of 3 and 4 pounder iron cannons, some of which have gun carriages and some without, but most of them are unusable. There still remain here from Mauritius dated the 1st of December, Anno 1692, two pieces of 2 pounder metal cannons, the gun carriages of which are also old and worm-eaten. On the left side, where the hill upon which this building rests rises up in height, stand some trees enclosed with palisades, where also some earth fruits grow. text_translated_detailed: most of them are unusable. There still remain here from Mauritius under date 1st December, Year 1692, two pieces of 2-pounder metal cannon, the carriages of which are also old and rotten. On the left side, where the cliff upon which this building rests rises up, there stand some trees enclosed with palisades, where also some earth fruits grow, but everything, because the hand has been withdrawn from it (as was reported, due to weakness of personnel), currently resembles a wilderness. Around this structure one sees some blade-like houses, which are used as a beast stable, smithy, kitchen, slaughterhouse, cooperage, and dairy houses. The mill, which lies about half an hour from here at a river, has also been inspected and is likewise completely fallen into ruin, and the bridge, the water channel, the three sluice doors, the ship's rudder, the plates on one of its sides, the bakehouse lying as it rotates, and the outer wing for the mill are entirely unfit for use. Also, no piece of wood was found in reserve to repair it, so that it is impossible to work with it during this rainy season. We lack from Mauritius under date 11th December, Year 1692, also a mill maker, through which fault the same runs the risk of being completely washed away by the water flowing off during the rainy season. But in order to prevent the same as much as possible, we have already given orders for the cutting of the timber work necessary for its restoration, with which we hope, with the two carpenters we have here, to prevent the ruin of the aforementioned mill, which is very apparent. But whether the same can be brought into a state to grind is doubtful, and for that purpose a carpenter who understands himself in mill making is necessarily required, just as we have also already stationed the same on the Island.

text_translated_detailed: Pieter Abrahamsz van Schagerbrugghe and Jan Abrahamsz Schagen, both from Mauritius under date 1st December, Year 1692, masons, of whom the latter is lame, have already been assigned land by the former chief and promised their freedom, so that it will not be possible to continue them in service. The former chief Abraham Steen and Jacob Waer, who also went with the dove to Batavia, make with the three aforementioned a reduction of 6 persons in the old garrison, leaving the same still 11 in number, whereby the chief Diodati, Valkhaven as second, and still 12 men from the Cape who landed here with the dove, make up 25 white heads for the said garrison. The same are employed for the following services, namely: 1 miller who has oversight of the mills; 1 person as apothecary in the dispensary; 2 hunters who provide the daily food for the garrison; 2 who work on the vessels, which daily go to the great river for sweet potato transport service; 1 surgeon; 2 smiths; 1 coppersmith who also works with the smith; 1 salt cutter; the 11 heads that are transported from Mauritius under date 1st December, Year 1692, 11 heads per transport; 2 carpenters, daily busy with the repair of the vessels, et cetera; 1 wagon driver who daily drives with sweet potatoes from the flat land to the great river; 1 gardener who has oversight of the Company's garden both on the flat land and here; 2 who have oversight of the sweet potato land, who take care of digging this from the ground and laying it out; 2 of the trusted ones who are daily used for searching for ambergris, gray [uncertain: possibly a type of whale product], and visiting the beaches; 1 mason; 3 who must watch the guard in the lodge due to lack of more personnel, and are also employed for wood cutting and other services, leaving 2 corporal heads, Diodak or Valkhoven.

As for Mister Heinsius and myself, since we could not accomplish anything for the Company's service by remaining in Saldanha Bay, and our mutual great weakness, the land air, and remedies were most urgently required, we made use of the galiot the Joan to come to the Cape, leaving on the 15th of February in the Table Bay where we cast anchor. There the governor received us most courteously with daily attention to setting the necessary orders so that we could continue our journey to Batavia as speedily as possible. Your Excellency's great and esteemed government and persons, I wish all prosperity and blessing, with deep respect, with which &c. (signed below) Your Excellency's great and esteemed most humble and obedient servant, signed W. van Wijngaerden. Batavia. To the Noble Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor-General, and the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of India.

As for Mister Heinsius and myself, since we could not accomplish anything for the Company's service by remaining in Saldanha Bay, and our mutual great weakness, the land air, and remedies were most urgently required, we made use of the galiot the Joan to come to the Cape, leaving on the 15th of February in the Table Bay where we cast anchor. There the governor received us most courteously with daily attention to setting the necessary orders so that we could continue our journey to Batavia as speedily as possible. text_translated_detailed: From the Cape of Good Hope on the 26th of March in the year 1693. Esteemed, Earnest, Valiant, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Gentlemen, the Esteemed Mister and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, together with the Esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of India. — Received in duplicate on the 14th of June 1693 by the ships Bantam and Vosmeer. Commanding Gentlemen, With the return of the Yacht the Grijpvogel [Goshawk], your Excellencies' high Esteemed [persons] shall be able to perceive from the missive by the Esteemed Commander Joan van den Bergh, may he rest in peace, how far we had advanced by God's grace at that time, and since that time the occasion has not presented itself to greet your Excellencies' high Esteemed [persons] further, I show herein dutifully, as that with our five combined ships on the 25th and 26th of December of the past year we became stranded in the Inrhuijme [uncertain: original text], and we began our journey again in God's name toward the Cape of Good Hope, where on the 20th of March of the current year we happily arrived with four fleet-holding ships, namely Nederland, Reigersdael, Sion, and Dregterland, and there to our great joy we found lying the vessels Vosmeer, Bantam, From the Cape of Good Hope on the 26th of March in the year 1693. and Langewijk, which had arrived from the homeland, together with the Handboog and the fluyt Prinselandt, the latter having been separated from us on the 7th of February of the past year by harsh and bitter winds. text_translated_detailed: we did not have many dead or sick, having lost in total no more than 19 heads, namely: Nederland — 3 dead. Reigersdael — 7 dead. Sion — 3 dead. Princelandt — 3 dead. Dregterland — 4 dead. Handboog — 1 dead. Together 19 dead. Although on the 3rd of February past at midnight through an unavoidable accident the Chief Merchant and former Councillor of Justice Duivelaer went overboard and drowned, without anyone knowing how this happened. Likewise, Almighty God saw fit that on the 4th, the following evening, in the setting of the first watch, the Esteemed Commander Joan van den Bergh (not without our sorrow) departed from this world. Whereupon the next day, orders having been given, the broad council came together, and after the last rites had been performed for the aforementioned esteemed Commander, it was deliberated in the aforementioned council concerning the necessity of appointing another chief commander of this costly return fleet. Therefore, the considerations of the members having been heard back and forth, it came to pass that the aforementioned council was pleased to appoint my person to that position, but all provisionally until the safe arrival at the Cape of Good Hope, so that by the Esteemed Mister Governor Simon van der Stel further disposition could be made in this regard, just as on the 23rd of this current month by the aforementioned Esteemed Mister Simon van der Stel in the presence of the Esteemed Extraordinary Councillors of India, the gentlemen van Werkendam and Kenisius, I was absolutely appointed as chief commander of this costly return fleet.

On the 2nd of August it happened favorably that the ship De Voorboog, which departed on the 7th of April with Wageningen from Texel north of England and sailed together until approximately the Salt Islands, went nowhere else and encountered nothing bad on the journey, having sailed out with 184 persons, of which 15 died on the way and 40 tons — were brought to the hospital for healing. Meijdregt departed on the 18th of January from Goree, mounted with 138 persons alone, sailed and chose on the 21st of January at Portsmouth harbor, where the Company's ships Nightvogel, De Faam, Agatja, and Dageraad were found lying, and at the beginning of February there came to anchor with them the ship Driebergen, which together on the order of our gentlemen masters on the 19th of April From the Cape of Good Hope on the 23rd of August in the year 1693. departed from there and sailed around the north of England: remaining together until approximately the equator, when each did his best to reach this corner, and although Meijdregt was the worst sailed of all, yet it was fortunate for his companions, having arrived here having lost 7 men on the journey and loaded our hospital with 34 sick. Driebergen departed on the 23rd of January with 138 men from Texel alone, and shortly thereafter in Portsmouth, as we have said, choosing harbor, came here on the 12th of August to table haven, at anchor. It has lost 3 men on the journey through sickness and brought 28 sick and exhausted ashore. The gentlemen Directors at the Chamber Amsterdam have been pleased to authorize us by their writing of the 17th of January last past to be able to unload from Driebergen aforementioned such masts as we most need, so that the arriving ships, which might need them, shall not be left without, but since we find we still have 18 masts here in stock, and that in most circumstances we are less short of round wood, and that one can with difficulty unload the same from Driebergen From the Cape of Good Hope on the 23rd of August in the year 1693. —

text_translated_detailed: per the ship Nightevecht received on the 20th of September 1693. From the Cape of Good Hope on the 31st of August 1693. Batavia. To the Honorable Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Gentlemen Councilors of India. The Most Esteemed, Great and Honorable, Valiant, Wise, Prudent and Most Generous Mister and Honorable Gentlemen. Honorable, Great and Esteemed Gentlemen, the ships Driebergen and Mijdregt on the 27th of August departed from this Table Bay [Cape of Good Hope] to sea, have taken with them our letters of the 23rd of the same month directed to your Honors, and these few lines shall serve solely as an escort to the ship Nightevecht and the papers herewith being conveyed to your great Honors. The ship De Faem lies at anchor here in order to depart together with Nightevecht, and to continue its journey to Ceylon in accordance with our masters' orders, with thirty-five soldiers having been transferred here aboard the Agatha. To our regret we see from the Cape of Good Hope on the 31st of August in the year 1693 the ships Dageraad and Woggenum, of which we make mention in our last aforementioned writing, not yet appearing. We keep ourselves occupied day and night in order to unload the aforementioned Agatha, so that this vessel as quickly as possible may allow the ship Nightevecht to follow to Batavia; with which &c. (noted below) your Honors' most humble and obliged servants (signed) Simon van der Stel, Andries de Man, E. I. Simons, W. Paet, Adriaen van Rheede, L. van der Stel. In the margin: In the Castle of Good Hope on the 31st of August in the year 1693. Register of the Papers consigned by the Honorable Mister Simon van der Stel, Councilor Extraordinary of India and Governor at the Cape of Good Hope and his Council, and directed to the Honorable Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Gentlemen Councilors of India at Batavia dated the 26th of September in the year 1693. No.

Onse heeren meesters hebben 't selve tot den madagascaarsen slaven handel aengelegt, werwaert 't staet afgevaerdigt te werden, soo haest ons toegecomen sal sijn 't gunt - daer toe vereijst wert, en voornamentlijck schipper stierman en Chirurgijn in geseijden handel bedreven, en ons bij haer Ed:e hoog agtb: belooft. den 16:' september koos hier mede haven de hoeker sprinckhaer den 17:en maij uijt goerhee nevens 't schip keurvorst van beijeren 't seijl gegaen, hebbende benoorden schotlant en tot den 12:en Julij en op de hoofte der soute g eijlanden met malcanderen geseijlt als wanneer Van Caeb de goede Hoop den 26:' Septemb: 1693. snagts hem uijt 't gesigt verloor voert 21. text_translated_detailed: on the 19th of April it departed from there together with the ships Nigtevecht, the Fame, Mijdregt, Agatha and Driebergen to sea, with which it continued sailing until the 31st of May and to the latitude of 10 degrees north, when it separated from them, and on the 29th of June reached Cape Lopez Gonzales in the intention to provision itself with fresh water there, but since it found four strong French ships lying there, it was forced without deliberating long to turn the bow toward Annabón, and having lain at anchor there for only half an hour on the 3rd of July, it was swept away from the same due to severe weather. From the Cape of Good Hope on the 26th of September in the year 1693. In such a way that without the aforementioned assistance or any refreshment being obtained, it again turned back, and after much struggling on the 31st of August in Saint Helena's Bay, due to opposing current and wind, it fell into distress and lost from the same our sloop laden with fresh water and much more supplies, so that both arrived here at anchor on the 15th of September. On the journey it had 2 deaths and brings 7 sick to our hospital. text_translated_detailed: From the Cape of Good Hope on the 18th of October in the year 1693, to Batavia, to the Honorable Mister Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Gentlemen Councilors of India. Most Earnest, great honor, valiant, wise, and provident, per the ship Company William, and most generous Mister and Honorable Gentlemen, most great and honorable Sirs, the fluyt ship Agatha on the 2nd of October departed hence to sea, has taken with it our latest letter directed to Your Excellency's great honor to Batavia, arriving on the same day here to refresh and to encounter the English return ship Bertley Castle, carrying 180 men and 60 pieces of cannon, which departed from Madras on the 23rd of June, old style, hither bound. It was in the past year 1692 in August on its outbound voyage from London that it was here as well, as we reported to Your Excellency's great honor in our letter of the 30th of September 1692. It is noteworthy that since its departure from England until this day it has lost no more than 5 men through sickness, according to the statement of its officers. They were on the 4th of July with twelve of the Company's warships off Tegenapatnam, and not far from Fort Saint David came to anchor, which (as the rumors there ran) sought to meet Your Excellency's great honor's orders, in order to undertake something of consequence against the French, and most likely against their fortress and Comptoir of Pondicherry. On the 3rd of March from Mangalore three French warships of 60, 40, and 24 pieces returned to Europe, and another carrying a vice admiral's flag and 60 pieces would have arrived in Bengal in April of this year. Furthermore, they report to us that their ships Chère Seconde, Samson, Modena, and several others had to refresh at these places.
